The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

false_positives.candidate:
Allows adding guests to cancelled or already-completed bookings

After loading the booking there is no check on `booking.status`. A user can add guests to a `CANCELLED`, `REJECTED`, or past `ACCEPTED` booking. `sendAddGuestsEmails` will still send a 'guests added' notification and `updateCalendarAttendees` will still push an updated invite for an event that is no longer happening. Guard against `booking.status === BookingStatus.CANCELLED` (and arguably against bookings in the past).

Any existing attendee can add arbitrary third parties to a booking

Authorization allows the request if the user is the organizer OR an attendee:

```ts
const isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find((attendee) => attendee.email === user.email);
if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) { ... }
```

Combined with the dialog's unrestricted email entry, any original invitee can inject any third-party email into the booking, getting them full calendar details, organizer info, other attendees, and a meeting invitation without the organizer's consent. The organizer should normally be the only one (plus team admins/owners) permitted to add guests. This is a serious privacy/access-control issue.

Guests persisted to DB before calendar/email side-effects, with no rollback

The flow is: `prisma.booking.update` (commits new attendees) -> `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` -> `sendAddGuestsEmails` (wrapped only in a `console.log` on error). There is no transaction and no compensation. If `updateCalendarAttendees` throws (e.g., bad credentials, video provider error), the guests remain in the database but never receive an invite; the caller sees a TRPC error and may retry, creating duplicates. If email sending fails it is silently swallowed, so the UI reports success while the new guest never receives notification. Either wrap everything in a transaction with rollback, or reverse the order (validate-then-side-effect-then-persist) and surface failures properly.

New guests are inserted with empty name and the organizer's timezone/locale

Each new guest row is created with:

```ts
{ name: "", email: guest, timeZone: organizer.timeZone, locale: organizer.locale }
```

An empty `name` will render as a blank attendee in the UI (booking list, emails, calendar) and confuses no-show/dropdown flows. Also forcing the organizer's timezone/locale means the new guest's localized email content and meeting-time display are wrong. Either ask for a name in the dialog (it currently does not), or at minimum leave name nullable/derive a placeholder, and use a sensible default locale (e.g., `en`).

No automated tests for a new permission-sensitive mutation with email and calendar side-effects

The PR adds a new tRPC mutation `viewer.bookings.addGuests` that mutates the DB, calls calendar/video integrations, and dispatches emails. There are no unit tests, integration tests, or e2e tests included. Given the multiple authorization bugs (admin+owner check, attendee-as-actor, case-sensitive dedupe, wrong credentials) and side-effect ordering issues already found in this review, at minimum a test suite covering: (1) team admin can add, team member cannot; (2) attendee cannot add; (3) case-insensitive duplicate is rejected; (4) cancelled booking is rejected; (5) calendar/email failures are surfaced, must be added before merge.

Uses array index as React key for email fields

`value.map((field, index) => <li key={index}>...)`. When a user removes an item in the middle of the list, every input after it is re-bound to the wrong value (because React reuses the DOM and state by index). Use a stable key (e.g., the email value itself or a generated id) so removing index N doesn't corrupt the remaining inputs.

`booking?.userPrimaryEmail` is not a known Booking field

The calendar event uses `email: booking?.userPrimaryEmail ?? organizer.email`. The Prisma `Booking` model exposes `user` (relation) and `userId`, but I cannot find a `userPrimaryEmail` column on the Booking model in this diff's context. If it doesn't exist on `booking`, this will be `undefined` and the fallback `organizer.email` is used; otherwise the column may silently return `null` and bypass the intended primary-email selection. Verify the field exists; if not, drop the `??` or fetch from the user relation explicitly.

addGuests uses authedProcedure instead of bookingsProcedure

All sibling booking mutations in this router (`editLocation`) are wrapped with `bookingsProcedure` which presumably enforces booking-level authorization. `addGuests` uses the bare `authedProcedure`, leaving all access control to the handler. The handler has the permission bugs described above, so any logged-in user who can hit this endpoint relies entirely on a handler bug-free. Switch to `bookingsProcedure` for consistency and defense-in-depth.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No guard against concurrent cron execution; duplicate SMS and lost retryCount increments possible

The handler reads `unscheduledReminders`, calls the external `twilio.scheduleSMS`, and then updates `workflowReminder` in separate non-transactional steps. There is no lock, advisory mutex, or single-runner coordination. If two cron instances overlap (e.g., the previous run is still in flight when a new one starts, or this cron is invoked manually while a scheduled run is active), both will fetch the same unscheduled rows, both will call `twilio.scheduleSMS` (producing duplicate SMS messages for end users), and both will perform `update` based on the same `retryCount` snapshot so one increment is effectively a no-op. The newly added retry logic amplifies this: if retryCount increments are lost due to the race, a reminder may need more than 2 actual failures before being cleaned up, or conversely may be deleted after only one observed failure. At minimum, the handler should use an advisory lock keyed on the workflow step or use an idempotent update (`update where retryCount = <stale value>`) to make the increment safe.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteMany retryCount branch lacks method filter, can delete non-SMS reminders

The new OR clause in the cleanup deleteMany only filters by `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` on the second branch, with no `method` constraint. The first branch correctly restricts to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`, but the retryCount branch will match WorkflowReminder rows of any method (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) if their retryCount ever exceeds 1. While this PR only increments retryCount for SMS, this is a latent bug: any future code path (or out-of-band DB change) that pushes an EMAIL/WHATSAPP reminder's retryCount above 1 will cause it to be silently deleted by this SMS handler. The retry branch should be `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` to keep the cleanup semantically consistent with the rest of the handler, which only processes SMS.

false_positives.candidate:
Cleanup deletes reminders based on retryCount even when scheduledDate is still in the future

The new OR clause causes any WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 to be deleted regardless of its scheduledDate. So if SMS scheduling fails twice for a reminder that is still scheduled to fire hours or days in the future, the reminder is permanently dropped even though the event has not happened yet. This matches the PR description but is worth flagging: there is no alerting or metric when a future reminder is given up on, and no way to distinguish "transient Twilio failure" from "permanent bad phone number". Consider also classifying errors so permanent failures (e.g., invalid phone number from Twilio) are dropped immediately while transient ones use more retries, or at least log when a future-dated reminder is being dropped.

Error log does not identify which reminder failed

The catch block logs only `Error scheduling SMS with error ${error}`. It does not include the reminder id, booking uid, workflowStepId, scheduledDate, sendTo, or the prior retryCount value. When the new retry-and-delete flow drops a reminder (after retryCount > 1) there is no operator-visible trail of which reminder was deleted or why it was abandoned, which makes production debugging and audit of dropped SMS reminders very difficult. At minimum the log line should include the reminder id and the new retryCount.

No tests cover the new retry-count / cleanup behavior

The change introduces new persistence logic (a new column, conditional increment in two branches, and a new cleanup predicate) but no test files were added or updated. There is no coverage verifying: (a) `retryCount` is incremented when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy, (b) `retryCount` is incremented in the catch branch, (c) reminders with `retryCount > 1` are deleted regardless of scheduledDate, (d) past-dated SMS reminders without retries are still deleted, or (e) the off-by-one threshold (2 failures -> delete) matches the PR description. Without tests, regressions in the retry threshold or in the OR-clause semantics (e.g., the missing method filter noted above) can ship undetected.

true_positives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Org scope silently drops direct org members when there are no child teams

In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition`, `userIdsFromOrg` is set to `[]` whenever `teamsFromOrg.length === 0`, so the `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds` query is skipped entirely. `teamIds` already contains `options.orgId`, but the conditional means a user who is a direct member of the organization (membership row with `teamId = orgId`) but is not a member of any sub-team is never included. Their individual bookings (and any event-type-owned bookings they make) will be invisible in org-scope insights. The query should be executed unconditionally (or fall back to a direct membership lookup on `orgId`). The bug pre-existed in the WhereInput form but is reproduced verbatim in the new SQL, and the new tests do not cover the no-sub-teams case.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid-options test bypasses TypeScript via `null as any`

The constructor parameter is declared `options: InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` (required, non-null), but the test for "invalid options" passes `options: null as any` and relies on `safeParse` returning `{ success: false }` so `this.options` ends up `null` and `NOTHING_CONDITION` is produced. This hides a real design question: invalid options silently turn the caller into an unauthorized principal instead of throwing, which means a production bug that constructs an `InsightsBookingService` with a malformed `options` object would just return no data rather than fail loudly. The constructor should either throw on invalid input, or its type should be widened to `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions | null | undefined` so callers can express intent without resorting to `as any`. The current arrangement also means the runtime contract is weaker than the type signature suggests.

Org-scope test depends on undefined query/Set ordering

The org-scope assertion compares against literal array orderings `[testData.org.id, testData.team.id, team2.id, team3.id]` and `[testData.user.id, user2.id, user3.id]`. These come from `TeamRepository.findAllByParentId`, `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, and `Array.from(new Set(userIdsFromOrg))`. None of those queries specify `ORDER BY`, so the order is implementation-defined and can vary across PostgreSQL versions, under concurrent load, or with different planner settings. A `toEqual` on `Prisma.sql` template literals compares the embedded `.values` arrays by deep equality, so any reorder will fail the test. Either add deterministic ordering on the repository queries, or normalize both sides of the assertion (e.g. compare by `Set` membership, or use a helper that re-sorts the array values) so the test is not order-sensitive.

findMany method removed without updating callers

The `findMany` method that previously executed the authorization/filter query through `prisma.bookingTimeStatusDenormalized.findMany` has been removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions()` plus a `prisma.$queryRaw` interpolation. The integration test was migrated to the new shape, but no other callers are updated in this PR. If any HTTP route, tRPC procedure, scheduled job, or other service in the repository invokes `InsightsBookingService.findMany(...)`, those call sites will now fail to compile and/or at runtime. Either the call sites must be migrated in this PR or a transitional shim should be added so the change is non-breaking.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateManyByCredentialId invoked with empty data

`await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` passes an empty data object, which only does anything because Prisma auto-bumps `@updatedAt`. Without that hidden schema behavior this would be a no-op (or even a validation error in some Prisma versions), so the intent ('bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under this credential') is implicit and brittle. Pass the timestamp explicitly, e.g. `data: { updatedAt: new Date() }`, and document that the field exists at the call site.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BSD sed syntax breaks on Linux

The line `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses the BSD/macOS form `sed -i ''` where the empty argument is the backup-extension placeholder. On GNU sed (the default on the Linux/CI environments this repo targets), `-i ''` is parsed as `-i` followed by `''` and then `-E`, causing errors like `sed: can't read E: No such file or directory`, so the .env update silently fails and the rest of the script can't restore GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL. Detect the platform (e.g. `[[ $OSTYPE == darwin* ]] && sed_i() { sed -i '' "$@"; } || sed_i() { sed -i "$@"; }`) or use a portable alternative such as `sed -i.bak ... && rm "$ENV_FILE.bak"`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteCache throws plain Error instead of TRPCError

The handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")` directly. The other handlers in this package throw `TRPCError` with appropriate codes (e.g. NOT_FOUND, UNAUTHORIZED). Throwing a bare Error here skips tRPC's code propagation: the client receives an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR with a 500 status for what is really a 404 / 403, and the toast in CredentialActionsDropdown cannot distinguish 'not found' from 'permission denied' from a transient DB error. Switch to `throw new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND", message: "Credential not found or access denied" })`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Timestamp hard-coded to en-US locale

Inside the cache_status dropdown, the timestamp is rendered with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" }).format(...)`. The component already has access to useLocale() for translations, but forces every user to see dates in the US format regardless of their locale, browser preference, or the locale actually in use in the rest of the app. This is a regression for non-en-US users and breaks the i18n expectations of the project. Use the locale returned by useLocale() (or navigator.language fallback) instead of the hard-coded `"en-US"`.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status ignores expiry, marking stale rows as fresh

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds uses prisma.calendarCache.groupBy to find the most recent updatedAt for each credential, but it does not constrain expiresAt to be in the future. The UI displays a 'Cache Status' timestamp whenever a row exists, even when all matching rows are expired (cache TTL is 30 days, set in upsertCachedAvailability via CACHING_TIME). Because getCachedAvailability itself filters by expiresAt >= now, the user is shown what looks like valid cache data for credentials whose cache is actually invalid. Add `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }` to the where clause so the UI only surfaces still-valid cache.

DropdownMenuItem used for non-interactive cache info

The 'Cache Status' / 'Last updated' block (lines 84-97) is rendered inside a `<DropdownMenuItem className="focus:ring-muted">` even though it contains no actionable control - it is purely informational. Radix dropdown items are interactive elements that expect to be selectable, so making one that does nothing on click produces an a11y warning (role with no action/handler) and means a screen-reader user hears it as a menu choice they can activate. Use a non-interactive primitive such as a `<div>` or `<DropdownMenuLabel>` for the read-only cache status row and reserve DropdownMenuItem for the Delete cached data choice below.

Migration comment does not match SQL

The header comment warns: 'Added the required column `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty.' The actual SQL does add a default (`DEFAULT NOW()`), so the warning is wrong and will confuse whoever next reviews this migration or runs it against a non-empty table. Either remove the misleading warning or replace it with one that describes the actual safe approach (adding the column with a server-side default and back-filling existing rows).

deleteCache success does not invalidate connectedCalendars

After deleting the cache the mutation only shows a toast and calls onSuccess?.(); it never invalidates the viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars query. The sibling disconnectMutation on lines 53-65 explicitly invalidates utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars and utils.viewer.apps.integrations on settle, which keeps the dropdown and parent list in sync. The deletion path lacks the same invalidation, so after a successful Delete cached data the dropdown continues to render the 'Cache Status' row with the previous timestamp and the 'Delete cached data' item, and the parent's ConnectedCalendarList still shows the now-stale cacheUpdatedAt. Add an invalidate of utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars (and ideally utils.viewer.apps.integrations) in onSuccess or onSettled.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
try/catch around forEach with awaited async work is dead code

`originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach(...)` calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...)` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` without `await`, and both helpers internally wrap their work in try/catch and only log errors. No error from those calls can ever propagate into the surrounding `catch (error)` block at line 970, so the `log.error(...)` is unreachable for any real failure. This is misleading and hides the fact that the caller has no way to know whether a reminder was successfully cancelled. Either `await` each call inside a per-iteration try/catch, or have the helpers rethrow and the caller await them.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteScheduledEmailReminder immediateDelete path leaves DB unupdated

When `immediateDelete` is true, the function calls the SendGrid cancel API and then returns without updating or deleting the WorkflowReminder row in the database. The two other code paths (`!referenceId` and `immediateDelete === false`) both clean up the DB row, so this branch is inconsistent. As a result, callers using `immediateDelete=true` (e.g. reschedules in `handleNewBooking.ts`) leave orphan rows in `WorkflowReminder` that will only be cleaned up once `scheduledDate` is in the past. More importantly, because the row is never marked `cancelled=true`, the CRON in `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` (which only selects `where: { cancelled: true }`) cannot retry the SendGrid cancellation if the initial API call fails, so the original SendGrid problem (failed cancellations → emails still being sent) is only partially fixed. The fix is either to also set `cancelled: true` (or delete the row) in this branch, or to stop passing `immediateDelete=true` from callers where this matters (such as the reschedule path, which unlike the workflow delete path does not rely on a cascade to remove the row).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellation query does not filter by method

`prisma.workflowReminder.findMany` selects reminders where `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate <= now + 1h` but does not restrict to `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. Today only EMAIL reminders are marked `cancelled=true` (SMS reminders are deleted immediately via `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`), so this is latent, but the cron then unconditionally calls SendGrid's `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `batch_id: reminder.referenceId` on whatever it finds. If a future change ever marks an SMS reminder as cancelled, this code will try to cancel it via the email provider and may also `delete` it, losing the row. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` to the where clause for safety.

Catch block aborts all SendGrid cancellations on a single failure

The try/catch wraps the entire `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop. A single SendGrid API failure (4xx/5xx, network error, rate limit, etc.) aborts the loop and skips every subsequent cancellation in this CRON run, even though the per-iteration `await client.request(...)` and `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` are independent. There is also no partial cleanup: if the throw happens after some `workflowReminder.delete` calls have been pushed but before `await Promise.all(...)`, those prisma operations are left as fire-and-forget unhandled promises. The catch should be moved inside the loop so one failed reminder doesn't stop the rest, and the deletes should be awaited per iteration (or collected only after a successful cancel).

Reschedule uses immediateDelete=true, bypassing the new deferred-cancel mechanism

When a booking is rescheduled, the workflow reminders of the original booking are cancelled by calling `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)`. This is inconsistent with the new design (which only marks `cancelled=true` and lets the CRON actually cancel in SendGrid) and with the cancellation flow in `handleCancelBooking.ts`, which calls the same function without `immediateDelete`. Because `immediateDelete=true` does not mark the row `cancelled=true`, the CRON never picks it up and there is no retry if SendGrid's `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` fails — exactly the failure mode this PR is trying to fix. Reschedules will therefore continue to send the original reminder whenever SendGrid has any transient issue. The call should drop the third argument and rely on the same deferred approach as `handleCancelBooking.ts`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach(async ...) does not await calendar/video deletions

The code wraps the bookingRef iteration in `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })`. `Array.prototype.forEach` ignores the return value of its callback and does not await Promises, so the async callbacks (which now `await getCalendar(...)` and invoke `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` / `deleteMeeting(...)`) are fire-and-forget. The outer `Reschedule` function returns as soon as the synchronous work completes, before the calendar/video integrations have been cancelled. Previously these were synchronous calls; the async refactor turned them into background tasks. The booking row is updated to CANCELLED and `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` is awaited before these deletions actually run, which is a data-integrity regression (integrations can stay in sync with the old time slot after the DB has already been flipped). Replace the `forEach` with a sequential `for...of` (or `Promise.all(refs.map(...))`) so the deletions are awaited.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate: Sequential awaits in getVideoAdapters serialize module loads

forEach(async ...) does not await calendar/video deletions

Identical antipattern to vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })`. After making the inner callback async, forEach no longer awaits any of the calendar `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting` Promises. The `Reschedule` function continues running and the `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` is awaited before the integration deletions actually execute. Result: the booking is updated, the reschedule email goes out, and the function returns before the previous Google/Outlook/Zoom events are cancelled. Convert to a real awaited loop.

forEach(async ...) skips calendar/video cancellations on reschedule

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` does not await the async callback. Inside, the code `await`s `getCalendar(...)` and calls `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` and `deleteMeeting(...)`, but because forEach discards the returned Promise and does not block, the `requestReschedule` mutation can finish — sending `sendRequestRescheduleEmail`, webhooks, and returning to the caller — before any of the previous calendar/video entries are cancelled. Previously these calls were synchronous; the async conversion silently turned them into best-effort background work. Replace with `for (const bookingRef of bookingRefsFiltered) { ... }` or `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours end uses slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

In the new working-hours check in `checkIfIsAvailable`, `end` is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` — the same value as `start`. It should be `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()`. Consequence: the `end > workingHour.endTime` half of the condition can never trigger, so a slot that starts inside working hours but whose end spills past `workingHour.endTime` (e.g. working hours 09:00–17:00, slot 16:30–17:30) is incorrectly treated as inside working hours. With a 60-minute event this can return bookable slots that extend past the organizer's day.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === instead of isSame

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly-constructed Dayjs objects with strict equality. Dayjs objects are compared by reference, so this branch is unreachable. The intent appears to be "override has zero duration / is empty", which should be `…isSame(…)`. Consequence: an empty/zero-length date override is never short-circuited and the surrounding code falls through to the other boundary checks, which can produce wrong availability when start and end coincide.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override day match is compared in UTC, not organizer tz

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` compares two UTC-formatted dates. The date override is a calendar day in the organizer's timezone, and `slotStartTime` is in UTC. Around the day boundary (e.g. override on 2024-01-01 IST = 2023-12-31 18:30 UTC …) a slot on the correct local day can be compared against the wrong UTC date and the override will be silently ignored. Use the organizer's timezone for both sides of the comparison (e.g. `dayjs.tz(slotStartTime, organizerTimeZone).format(...)`).

New test asserts same UTC slots for two different invitee timezones

The new `scheduleForEventOnADayWithDateOverrideDifferentTimezone` case calls `getSchedule` with `timeZone: "Asia/Dhaka"` and expects the identical UTC slots `[08:30, 09:30, 10:30, 11:30]` as the IST case, with the comment "it should return the same as this is the utc time". The PR description says the fix makes date overrides adjust to the attendee's timezone, so two invitees in materially different timezones (e.g. IST vs America/Los_Angeles) should see different UTC slots. The test as written locks in the pre-fix behavior and will not catch a regression of the stated bug; it also only spans a 30-minute tz difference which doesn't expose the problem at all.

Override boundary check is strict, missing same-instant starts

`slotStartTime.isAfter(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` is strict: a slot whose start equals the override end is not filtered, and slots that straddle the override end (e.g. override 14:00–18:00, slot 17:30–18:30) are also not filtered because there is no check that the slot end is within the override. The check should also require `slotStartTime` not to be after `date.end` (use `isSameOrAfter` or also verify the slot end) and the same boundary issue applies to `date.start` (a slot that begins before the override starts but ends inside it slips through).

Working-hours day/hour/minute read from UTC, not organizer tz

`slotStartTime` is `time.utc()`, so `slotStartTime.day()`, `.hour()` and `.minute()` return UTC values, while `workingHours` are stored in the organizer's timezone. The membership check `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` and the minute comparison will be wrong near day boundaries or for organizers not in UTC (e.g. a slot at 23:30 IST = 18:00 UTC will be checked against the UTC day/hour instead of the IST day/hour). This can return slots outside the organizer's working day or filter out slots that should be available.

checkIfIsAvailable ignores override.timeZone, uses caller-supplied organizerTimeZone

`dateOverrides` are flattened with `timeZone: availability.timeZone` attached, but `checkIfIsAvailable`'s signature drops that field (type is `{ start: Date; end: Date }[]`) and instead uses the caller-supplied `organizerTimeZone` to compute the UTC offset for `date.start`. If a date override was created in a timezone different from the one currently passed as `organizerTimeZone` (e.g. round-robin where a fixed host's override was stored with one tz and `schedule.timeZone` resolves to another, or DST boundary), the override's intended local time will be misinterpreted, returning the wrong availability.

override startTime/endTime computed in UTC, not invitee local time

`dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + …` produces the hour/minute of the shifted UTC instant, but the surrounding `buildSlots` compares these values to `dayStart` which is in the invitee's local timezone. The result is that for two invitees in different timezones the same `startTime` value yields the same UTC slot, regardless of invitee tz. This is exactly the behavior the PR description claims to fix ("date overrides didn't adjust to different timezones"). The correct computation is the override's start in the invitee's local tz, e.g. `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).hour() * 60 + dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).minute()`.

override.start.toString() parsed in server local tz, then re-zoned

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` first stringifies a Date (which embeds the server's local timezone offset) and parses it back, then re-zones. The resulting `utcOffset` depends on the server's TZ rather than being a pure UTC interpretation. On any server not running in UTC the organizer/invitee offset values (and therefore the computed `offset` and the resulting `startTime`/`endTime`) will be wrong. Use `dayjs.utc(override.start)` (or pass the Date directly) before `.tz(...)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError possible if Integration has no 'sender' in metadata

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch the user-mismatch check reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. Existing Integration rows created before this PR shipped (or rows created via paths that don't populate `sender`, e.g., legacy migrations) will have no `sender` key in `metadata`, raising `KeyError` and surfacing a 500 instead of the intended error page. The check should be guarded — e.g., treat a missing `sender` as a failed validation (`return error(...)`) or use `.get()` with a default. Otherwise the new security check will break upgrades.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Hardcoded HMAC signature will mismatch the modified body

In `test_github_user_mismatch` the webhook is posted with the hardcoded header `HTTP_X_HUB_SIGNATURE="sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486"`, but the request body is `json.dumps(webhook_event)` after the test mutates `installation.id` and `sender.login`. That HMAC was presumably computed over the unmodified `INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE` bytes. Standard GitHub webhook handlers verify the signature against the raw request body and reject mismatches (typically with a 401/403). When the handler rejects the webhook, no `Integration` record with `sender.login == "attacker"` is created, and the subsequent user-mismatch check in `GitHubInstallation` won't fire as intended. Either compute the signature dynamically from the mutated payload using the test webhook secret, or fix the signature for the actual bytes posted. This test should currently be failing or is silently broken.

No tests for the new OAuth error branches

OAuthLoginView introduces four new error branches that all funnel into the same `error()` helper and are therefore indistinguishable to callers: (1) `state` parameter mismatch, (2) GitHub returning no `access_token` in the token-exchange response, (3) `get_user_info` returning no `login`, and (4) the GitHubInstallation-level user mismatch (which is tested but only via the generic template assertion). Each of these is a distinct failure mode documented in the PR description ("state mismatch", "wrong or re-used code", "authenticate user mismatch") and should have a dedicated test that verifies the request reaches the expected code path and that the failure is rendered. The current `test_github_user_mismatch` only asserts `b"Invalid installation request."` and doesn't distinguish user mismatch from a state or token failure.

OAuth authorize URL parameters not URL-encoded

The OAuth authorize URL is built via f-string interpolation: `f"{...}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"`. Neither `state` (currently `pipeline.signature`, an md5 hex digest, so safe today) nor `redirect_uri` is URL-encoded. If `redirect_uri` ever contains reserved characters (`&`, `?`, `=`, `#`, etc.), or if `pipeline.signature` generation changes, GitHub will parse the query string incorrectly and the OAuth callback state verification will fail or — worse — allow query parameters to bleed into `state`/`redirect_uri`. Use `urllib.parse.urlencode` for the query string.

OAuth scope not requested, but no scope validation either

OAuthLoginView does not include a `scope` parameter when redirecting to GitHub's authorize URL. The access token returned will have only the default user:email scope (or whatever GitHub grants by default). `get_user_info` only uses `/user`, which works under the default scope, but if Sentry ever tries to use the resulting token for anything requiring an additional scope (e.g., reading private email, listing org installations), the request will silently 404/403. This is informational; consider either requesting the scopes Sentry actually needs explicitly (`scope=user:email read:org`), or documenting that only the default user-scope token is intended.

safe_urlopen() not wrapped in try/except

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch(), `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is called OUTSIDE the try/except block. Network errors, DNS failures, connection timeouts, or GitHub returning 5xx will raise an exception and produce a generic 500 error page instead of the user-friendly error page rendered by the `error()` helper. The try/except block below only covers `safe_urlread`, `decode`, and `parse_qsl` failures. The same applies to `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` at line 434 — any exception there will also bubble up as a 500. Both calls should be wrapped so transient failures degrade gracefully.

test_installation_not_found doesn't exercise the 404 path

The test is named `test_installation_not_found` and stubs `/app/installations/{installation_id}` to return 404, but the assertion only checks for the generic "Invalid installation request." string. Tracing the flow: the first request to `setup_path` with `installation_id` triggers OAuthLoginView, which redirects to GitHub (no call to the 404 endpoint). false_positives.candidate:
Class docstring says 'one process per shard' but the implementation creates up to `max_processes`

The updated docstring states 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing', but the constructor takes `max_processes` and defaults it to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. A consumer configured with `--flusher-processes=2` and four shards will create 2 processes, each handling 2 shards. The docstring is therefore misleading; describe the actual semantics (e.g., 'creates up to `max_processes` worker processes, each handling one or more Redis shards').

Dead method `_create_process_for_shard` is never invoked

The method `_create_process_for_shard` (lines 127-132) is defined but never called anywhere in the file or by any caller. The corresponding `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) is the one used by `_create_processes` and `_ensure_processes_alive`. Either delete the dead method or wire it up — leaving it in production code is misleading and means future maintainers will assume shard-level restart is supported when it is not.

Old flusher process is not joined before spawning its replacement

`_ensure_processes_alive` calls `process.kill()` and then immediately calls `_create_process_for_shards`, which spawns a new `SpawnProcess` and stores it in `self.processes[process_index]`. `kill()` only sends SIGKILL; it does not wait for the OS to actually reap the process. Until the old process is reaped it can still be inside its main loop, still flushing segments from Redis and still mutating the shared `process_healthy_since` / `process_backpressure_since` `Value`s. Once the new process is up, both processes will flush the same shards concurrently, producing duplicate Kafka payloads on `BUFFERED_SEGMENTS` (idempotency assumptions in downstream consumers are likely broken) and racing on the shared `Value`s. Call `process.join(timeout)` (with a short timeout) before spawning the replacement, or use `process.terminate()` followed by `join()` to give it a chance to exit cleanly first.

`MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` allows 11 restarts instead of the 10 the name suggests

The check is `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS:` and the counter is incremented after the check. So the counter can take the values 0..10 with the check still False, then 11 with the check True. That means the consumer will restart an unhealthy flusher process 11 times before crashing, not 10 as the constant name and original semantics imply. Either rename the constant, change the check to `>=`, or move the increment before the check.

`max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` silently treats 0 as None

The `or` falls back to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` whenever `max_processes` is falsy. Passing `max_processes=0` (e.g., to explicitly disable the flusher) will instead spin up a process per shard. Use `if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` so that 0 is honored. Additionally, with `num_processes = 0`, the subsequent `for i, shard in enumerate(...): process_index = i % 0` would raise ZeroDivisionError — there is no input validation guarding this.

`process_restarts` counter never resets, so a long-running consumer is doomed by transient crashes

`self.process_restarts[process_index]` is initialized to 0 in `__init__` and only ever incremented in `_ensure_processes_alive`; it is never reset on successful operation. For a long-lived consumer that is rebalanced occasionally and where the SpanFlusher is reconstructed, this is bounded, but the per-process restart counter is shared across the lifetime of the SpanFlusher object. A single flusher that crashes 11 times over the course of days for transient reasons (deploys, brief OOM kills, broker hiccups) will permanently take down the consumer with no path to recovery short of a full restart. Consider resetting the counter once the process has been healthy for a sustained period.

`process_restarts` is incremented before the restart attempt, so failed restarts consume the budget

The order in `_ensure_processes_alive` is: check `> MAX`, increment, then `process.kill()` and `_create_process_for_shards(...)`. If `_create_process_for_shards` raises (e.g., OS resource exhaustion, pickling error), the counter has already been incremented and the next health check will be one step closer to crashing the consumer despite no successful restart ever having occurred. Move the increment to after a successful recreation, or wrap the restart in try/except and only increment on success.

`test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts setup, not that flushing actually works

The new test only verifies that `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes == 2`, `num_processes == 2`, and that 4 shards are distributed. It does not submit any spans, so it cannot catch regressions where the per-process buffers route reads to the wrong Redis keys, where the multiprocessing Value objects are misbound, where restart logic corrupts `process_to_shards_map`, or where flushes are silently dropped because a process never sees data assigned to its shards. Extend the test to submit spans to at least two different shards and assert they reach the pipe, ideally with assertions that each process only flushed its assigned shards.

false_positives.candidate:
Failed messages are silently lost on processing exception

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, the `finally` clause unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` regardless of whether `result_processor` raised. The exception is caught and logged by the inner `except Exception`, but the offset is still marked complete, then committed to Kafka by the commit loop. The message is then gone and will not be retried on restart. This contradicts the strategy's docstring which promises "Only commits offsets after successful processing" and is a serious data integrity issue (e.g., missed uptime check results, missed monitor check-ins). Either the complete_offset must be conditional on success (e.g., a success flag set in the try), or failed messages must be routed to a DLQ. The existing batched-parallel path uses ThreadPoolExecutor.submit which silently captures exceptions, so it has the same data-loss pattern; this PR replicates and deepens the problem for the new mode.

Shutdown ordering can cause workers to exit before draining queues

In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`, `worker.shutdown = True` is set on all workers BEFORE `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called on each queue. The worker loop is `while not self.shutdown: try: work_queue.get() ...`, so a worker that just finished processing one item and is returning to the top of the loop will observe `self.shutdown == True` and exit without ever pulling the next item from its queue. Because the workers have already exited by the time `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` runs, the items left in each queue are never drained and are silently discarded (only re-read from Kafka on next start, if not yet committed). The `worker.shutdown = True` step is also redundant: `q.shutdown()` is sufficient to terminate the workers via the `queue.ShutDown` exception. Remove the `worker.shutdown = True` loop (or move it after the join), so that `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` can actually drain pending items.

hash() randomization breaks ordering guarantee across restarts

`FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` returns `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). After any restart or new worker process, the same group_key can map to a different queue, violating the documented "Items for the same group are processed in order" guarantee. Example: if the consumer dies after submitting offset N to queue 5 and is restarted, offset N+1 for the same group may be hashed to queue 7 and processed in parallel/independently from any later retry of offset N, breaking in-order processing. Use a stable, cross-process hash like `int(hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)` (or `hashlib.sha256(...)`) instead of `hash()`.

The test should explicitly set `direction: LokiQueryDirection.Scan` to match the established convention and to ensure deterministic behavior.

Redundant applyTemplateVariables calls in shard splitting flow

When shard splitting is active, runShardSplitQuery calls applyTemplateVariables on each target (line 52 of shardQuerySplitting.ts), then for every shard group runSplitQuery is invoked which calls applyTemplateVariables again on the same targets (line 299 of querySplitting.ts). This is confirmed by the test 'Interpolates queries before running' which expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times = 1 (in runShardSplitQuery) + 4 (one per shard group in runSplitQuery). For idempotent interpolation this is functionally correct but wasteful; any non-idempotent side effects in applyTemplateVariables (logging, analytics) would occur twice. The redundant call could be avoided by either skipping applyTemplateVariables in runSplitQuery when called from runShardSplitQuery, or by not re-interpolating in the inner runSplitQuery call.

The new code calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` on items of `request.targets` directly. Standard implementations of `applyTemplateVariables` mutate the input query and return it (as evidenced by the test mock at shardQuerySplitting.test.ts lines 56-59). This means the caller's `request.targets[i]` will have its `expr` and `step` mutated to interpolated values as a side effect of running split queries. If the caller (or downstream code) inspects `request.targets` after `runSplitQuery`/`runShardSplitQuery` returns, it will see the interpolated values rather than the original template expressions. This is the same behavior as the previous `interpolateVariablesInQueries` call, but worth noting that the original request object is no longer pristine after splitting.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit can be exceeded under concurrent load (TOCTOU)

In CreateOrUpdateDevice, the active device count is read with CountDevices and then, based on that single read, either an UPDATE or an INSERT path is taken. There is no row-level lock, advisory lock, or transactional serialization between the count and the subsequent write. Under concurrent requests from different device IDs, two goroutines can both observe count == limit-1, both fall through to the INSERT path, and the resulting row count exceeds the configured AnonymousDeviceLimit. The whole point of this PR is the limit; it must hold under concurrency. Fix by serializing the check+write (e.g. transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a sentinel row, an advisory lock, or pushing the limit enforcement into a single atomic SQL statement).

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Anonymous auth now blocks on DB write and request context cancellation

Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine on a fresh context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute) so anonymous authentication never waited on, nor could be aborted by, the DB. The new code calls TagDevice(ctx, ...) synchronously, using the request context. Consequences: (1) every anonymous auth now incurs at least one DB round-trip (CountDevices, plus UPDATE or INSERT) before the identity is returned, (2) if the client disconnects mid-request the request context is cancelled and the tag DB write fails with context.Canceled, (3) any DB slowness or transient error directly delays/fails anonymous logins. The goroutine-and-detached-context design existed precisely to decouple auth from the side-effect DB write. The limit check needed to make auth decisions could be done as a separate read-only query while still keeping the write detached; or the limit check could run in the goroutine and short-circuit a follow-up call.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Returning devices whose entry is expired are wrongly rejected as 'limit reached'

updateDevice issues `UPDATE anon_device SET ... WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?`, where the BETWEEN range is `device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration)` to `device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(time.Minute)` (i.e. the last 30 days). CountDevices uses the same window, so any device whose updated_at is older than 30 days is NOT counted in the active device count. But the UPDATE WHERE clause filters out that exact row, returning 0 rowsAffected and surfacing ErrDeviceLimitReached. Effect: a returning user whose anon_device row is between 30 and 61 days old (the cleanup interval is 61 days) is denied authentication even though, by the counting rule, there is 'room' for them. The intent of the limit appears to be 'only NEW device_ids are limited; existing device_ids are always updatable'. Match on device_id alone, or look the device up first, before deciding to reject.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

```

...
```

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Undocumented 10x ticker frequency change affects all cleanup jobs

The cleanup ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute:
```

+ ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)
```
This is not mentioned in the PR description and is unrelated to the MySQL deadlock fix. It increases the run frequency of *every* job in clean() (tmp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) by 10x, multiplying DB load and the chance of overlapping long-running cleanups against the 9-minute per-cycle timeout. If the change is intentional (e.g. to compensate for accumulation during the deadlock period), it needs its own justification, and the PR description and release notes must call it out so operators can adjust. Nil error logged as err field on success

Multiple new log calls include `"err", err` after the error has already been checked and returned (e.g. lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). On the happy path err is nil, so the resulting structured log entry looks like `"err": null` for a successful batch. This is misleading to operators who scan logs for `"err":` fields and makes it look like every cleanup batch is failing. The err key should only be included when an error is actually present.

O(n^2) string building in SQLite large-batch path

The SQLite parameter-limit workaround builds the IN-list with repeated fmt.Sprintf:
```
values := fmt.Sprint(ids[0])
for _, v := range ids[1:] {
    values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)
}
```
This is O(n^2) in both time and allocations because each step copies the entire growing string. With the batch size used in the new test (32767) this is tens of millions of bytes copied. The same job can be done in O(n) with a strings.Builder and strconv.AppendInt. The path is also only triggered when batch size exceeds the SQLite parameter limit, so it is exercised by the new integration test and the cost matters.

fetchIDs concatenates table name and condition into SQL

fetchIDs builds SQL via fmt.Sprintf with the table name and the WHERE clause as opaque strings:
```
sql := fmt.Sprintf(`SELECT id FROM %s`, table)
sql += fmt.Sprintf(` WHERE %s`, condition)
```
Today every call site passes a constant string so there is no immediate injection, but the signature invites future callers to pass user-controlled fragments. Either make the table an enumerated constant or compose the predicate through bound parameters, so the function cannot be misused.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete sets klog context with d.Log instead of enriched log

Create/Get/List/Update/DeleteCollection all do `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` using the `log` variable enriched via `WithValues("name", ..., "kind", ..., "method", ...)`. It should use the enriched `log` variable.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection records storage metric for legacy call

In the DeleteCollection async goroutine, `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` is called after `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)`. It should be `d.recordLegacyDuration` because the call is to LegacyStorage, not Storage. As written, every legacy delete-collection failure will be misattributed to Storage in metrics, defeating monitoring and SLO alerting on the legacy path.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records storage metric with name as kind label

In Delete, the success-path metric is `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. All other methods use `options.Kind` as the third argument (the resource-kind label). Passing `name` here will produce a different label cardinality and break any dashboard or alert that aggregates by kind for delete operations. It should be `options.Kind` to be consistent with Create/Update/DeleteCollection and with the legacy-error metric on line 113.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy goroutines have no panic recovery

The four `go func()` blocks (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) call into legacy storage and record metrics without any panic recovery. A panic inside the legacy storage adapter or in the metric call will crash the process because Go panics in unrecovered goroutines are fatal. Each goroutine should at minimum `defer recover()` and log the recovered value so that a single failing legacy backend cannot bring down the API server.

Async legacy write derives context from cancelled request context

All four async goroutines (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) build their timeout context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the request context (`klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` from the outer function). When the originating HTTP handler returns, the request context is cancelled and the derived context is immediately cancelled as well, so the 10s timeout is effectively zero. The whole point of mode 3 is to mirror writes to legacy as a safety net; with a cancelled parent context this safety net is dropped on every request that returns before the goroutine schedules. The legacy-mirror call should be made independent of request lifetime (e.g., derive from a long-lived background context) so that the write actually completes after the response is sent.

Create error path records legacy metric using storage timer

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Two problems: (1) it records a legacy duration even though the legacy was never called; (2) the duration it computes is for Storage (startStorage), not Legacy. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. The same bug exists for Update on line 129. Effect: storage failures will be miscounted as legacy failures and the recorded duration will not correspond to the failing call.

Legacy mirror timeout is a hardcoded magic number

`time.Second*10` appears as the timeout for the legacy-mirror context in Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. This should be a configurable constant (or a field on DualWriterMode3) so it can be tuned per resource type and tested; otherwise changing it requires editing four call sites.

Same objInfo reused for Storage and Legacy Update calls

`objInfo` is passed to `d.Storage.Update` and then, in the goroutine, to `d.Legacy.Update` unchanged. `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations are commonly stateful (the previous version of this file explicitly wrapped it in `updateWrapper` and supplied a fresh wrapper holding the updated object for the legacy call). Reusing objInfo risks the legacy update either re-fetching the pre-update object, returning stale data, or returning an error from the second `UpdatedObject` invocation. This is a behavioural regression from the prior implementation in this same function.

TestMode3_Create failure case sets up the wrong store's mock

The second test case in TestMode3_Create is named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" and expects `wantErr: true`, but the expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` against the legacy store. Because the test wires both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` to the same `mock.Mock{}`, the expectation ends up firing on whichever call runs first (the storage call), so the test happens to pass for the wrong reason. If the two mocks are ever given separate mock instances, this case will silently flip to passing on the legacy path and the error will be swallowed by the async goroutine. Either rename the case or register the expectation against the storage mock explicitly.

TestMode3_Get uses local prometheus registry instead of shared one

Only `TestMode3_Get` creates its own registry with `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()`. Every other TestMode3_* test uses the package-level `p`. The dual-writer change in `dualwriter_mode1_test.go` removed the same leftover in mode1, but the corresponding cleanup was missed in `TestMode3_Get`. Use the shared `p` for consistency and to avoid duplicate registries across tests.

Tests do not verify async legacy write actually occurred

In TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection the legacy call is dispatched in a goroutine after the request returns, but the test only asserts on the synchronous return value. There is no synchronization (no WaitGroup, channel, or `m.AssertExpectations`) to ensure the legacy mock was actually invoked before the test exits. A regression where the goroutine no longer runs (e.g., refactor that accidentally makes the legacy call synchronous-but-skipped) would pass these tests silently. Add a synchronization mechanism (e.g., a `sync.WaitGroup` toggled in the goroutine, or use a channel signaled by a mock callback) and call `m.AssertExpectations(t)` to assert the legacy side effect actually happened.

Update error path records legacy metric using storage timer

When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Same issue as the Create error path: this should be `d.recordStorageDuration` because the error happened in Storage, and the timer being measured (`startStorage`) corresponds to Storage, not Legacy. Storage update failures will be misattributed to the legacy path in metrics.

defer cancel() placed after side-effecting line in Update goroutine

In the Update goroutine, `defer cancel()` is placed between `startLegacy := time.Now()` and the `d.Legacy.Update` call. While functionally correct (defer runs at function exit), it is stylistically inconsistent with the Create/Delete/DeleteCollection goroutines, which put `defer cancel()` immediately after the `context.WithTimeoutCause` call. Easy fix: move the deferred cancel directly under the WithTimeoutCause call.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Thundering herd: no re-check of cache after acquiring write lock

After acquiring the write lock at line 48, the function does not re-check whether entryPointAssetsCache has been populated by another goroutine that passed the fast-path check (lines 41-47) while the cache was still nil. As a result, every concurrent goroutine that observes a nil cache in the fast path will acquire the write lock in turn and each redundantly re-read the manifest file and re-parse the JSON. This is the classic double-checked-locking pitfall: the fast-path RLock/RUnlock check at lines 41-43 is not mirrored inside the Lock-held critical section. At Grafana startup, where many HTTP handlers can call this function concurrently, this causes N redundant file reads and JSON decodes instead of one. The fix is to add a re-check inside the write-lock critical section, e.g. by inserting `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` on line 48.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test added for the race fix

The PR fixes a data race on the entryPointAssetsCache package variable by adding a sync.RWMutex around its reads and writes. However, no test file is added or modified alongside this change. A regression test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently from multiple goroutines (e.g. via sync.WaitGroup) and runs under `go test -race` would have caught the original race and now guards against future refactors reintroducing it. true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

Error message claims SQL expressions were never implemented

When `enableSqlExpressions` returns false, the reader returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. No regression test that SQL expressions are rejected

`pkg/expr/sql/db.go` introduces an empty `DB` struct whose three methods all return `errors.New("not implemented")`, and is wired into `parser.go` and `sql_command.go`. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer serializes per key — duplicate indexes possible

The previous version held `b.cacheMu` for the entire BuildIndex call, so concurrent calls for the same key were serialized and the cached index was consistent. The new version only locks when assigning `b.cache[key] = idx`. Two concurrent calls to `BuildIndex` for the same `NamespacedResource` (for example, two simultaneous `Search` requests that both find the cache empty via `getOrCreateIndex`, or the init goroutine racing with an incoming search) will both:
  1. Open separate bleve indexes (file or memory),
  2. Run the builder to write all documents,
  3. Flush,
  4. Race to write `b.cache[key]` — last writer wins, the loser's index is orphaned in memory and the work is wasted.
The PR description frames this as "finer grain locking", but the same-key duplication problem is exactly the TODO called out in `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` ("We want to block while building the index and return the same index for the key … simple mutex not great … we don't want to block while anything in building, just the same key"). A per-key lock (e.g. a `sync.Map` of in-progress builds, or a sharded mutex keyed by `NamespacedResource`) is needed to actually fix the duplicate-build race while keeping different-key concurrency.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Eager Init inside NewResourceServer changes the constructor's contract

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously before returning. The constructor will now block for the full duration of search-index build (potentially many seconds for large installations) and return an error if init fails. Previously the same errors would surface on the first RPC and the constructor returned quickly.
This breaks any caller that expected the constructor to be cheap (tests, callers that wire up dependencies lazily, callers that want to surface a degraded server, callers that explicitly rely on `server.Init` being invoked separately). The PR description itself flags this concern ("Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily? What could this break?") without answering it. Verify all callers of `NewResourceServer` and the SQL `NewBackend` (which now also returns only after `Init` succeeds, since its backend implements the resource LifecycleHooks path) before merging — at minimum, document the contract change on the function and make sure module startup won't now fail outright where it previously degraded.
