Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

false_positives.candidate:
remove() unconditionally hits the DB to fetch the IDP

The diff hoists `IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` out of the `if (isInvalid(cacheKey))` branch so the result can be passed to the new `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` call. As a consequence, every `remove(alias)` now performs a JPA `getByAlias` lookup, even when the IDP is fully cached in `CachedIdentityProvider`. Previously the DB was only hit on the invalidation path or on a cache miss; the cache-hit path was DB-free. The login-eligibility check can be satisfied by reusing the cached model (e.g. `cached != null ? cached.getIdentityProvider() : idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)`), so this regression is avoidable without losing the new invalidation behaviour.

searchKey for REALM_ONLY mode varies with organizationId unnecessarily

In `getForLogin`, `String searchKey = organizationId != null ? organizationId : "";` is used for every `FetchMode`, but `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` does not depend on `organizationId` (the default implementation always sets `ORGANIZATION_ID` to null for that mode, so the result set is identical regardless of the orgId parameter). Calls to `getForLogin(REALM_ONLY, ...)` with different non-null organizationIds will miss the searchKey inside the cached `IdentityProviderListQuery`, fall into the `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)`/re-query path, and accumulate redundant searchKeys in the same cached entry. The searchKey for `REALM_ONLY` should be a constant (e.g. always `""`) so all REALM_ONLY lookups share one cached entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns default JCE provider, not BouncyCastle

The implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the JDK provider that happens to supply the default keystore type (typically SUN/SunJCE), not BouncyCastle. Every other CryptoProvider implementation returns a BouncyCastle/FIPS provider here (DefaultCryptoProvider returns bcProvider, FIPS1402Provider returns bcFipsProvider), and the interface Javadoc on CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() explicitly states 'BouncyCastle security provider'. Callers that rely on this getter to obtain a BC-backed Provider will silently receive the JDK provider instead, which can cause missing algorithms, wrong defaults (e.g., signature/padding), or NPEs in downstream code that assumed non-null BC.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code allocates and discards two ASN1Encoders in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 ('ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);') create two encoders, allocate ByteArrayOutputStream buffers, write the BigIntegers, and immediately discard the results. They are not stored and not part of the DER sequence produced below. They are pure waste (two extra BigInteger.toByteArray() calls and allocations on every ECDSA sign/verify) and clearly look like a leftover from refactoring. They should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() added as non-default method breaks third-party CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public interface in org.keycloak.common.crypto that is implemented by external modules (default/elytron/fips1402) and is part of the published keycloak-common artifact. Adding 'int order();' as an abstract method (instead of a default method) is an ABI break: every third-party or downstream implementation of CryptoProvider will fail to compile against the new release. Since the only purpose of order() is to pick between multiple implementations on the classpath, it should be 'default int order() { return 0; }' (or similar) so existing implementations keep working and the new AuthzClientCryptoProvider can opt in to a lower priority.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ECDSA conversion test only round-trips, does not validate against known vectors or wrong-key cases

ECDSAAlgorithmTest always generates a default-curve (P-256) EC key and runs the same round-trip (DER -> RS -> DER -> RS, equality) for ES256/ES384/ES512. This will pass even if the converter silently produces wrong-length outputs, drops leading bytes incorrectly for edge cases (r or s near q/2, r with high bit set, leading 0x00 from DER INTEGER), or works only because the specific test key avoids boundary values. There is also no test asserting the size of the produced concatenated/DER output, no negative-case test (truncated, malformed), and no test that exercises getBouncyCastleProvider/getKeyStore (whose implementation is actually wrong, see separate finding). Tests against a known signature vector per curve would catch real conversion bugs.

logger.debugf used with a preformatted message and no parameters

The new debug branch builds a StringBuilder of ignored provider names and then calls 'logger.debugf(builder.toString())'. debugf is the parameterized-format API; passing a plain string with no parameters means the string is treated as a format and any stray '%' would throw. It should be 'logger.debug(builder.toString())' (or 'logger.debugf("Ignored crypto providers: %s", joined)'). Same anti-pattern is present on line 63 which is pre-existing but worth aligning.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission only enumerates the "all-clients" resource and misses individual client resources

`getClientsWithPermission(String scope)` iterates with `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)`. Only the type-resource created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.init` (with type "Clients") matches this query, because `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` creates per-client resources without setting the `type` field (the `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())` call never sets a type). Therefore (a) when a user has permission only via a per-client resource, `getClientsWithPermission` returns an empty set, and (b) when the user has an "all-clients" grant, the result contains the literal name "Clients" instead of the actual client IDs in the realm. Either the per-client resources must be created with `type = CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE`, or the enumeration should iterate all client resources (e.g., `resourceStore.findByName(server, ...)` for each client, or by a different store query).

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NPE in hasPermission when the "all-clients" resource does not exist

In `hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope)`, when no per-client resource exists, the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)`. That method can return null (e.g., schema not yet initialized, `supportsAuthorizationSchema` returns false, unknown resource type, or `findByName` returns no row). The result is then passed unchecked to `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)`, which dereferences the resource (e.g., to read its id) and will throw NullPointerException. A null check is required before invoking `findByResource`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Several imports and a private helper are unused

The imports `org.jboss.logging.Logger`, `org.keycloak.authorization.common.ClientModelIdentity`, `org.keycloak.authorization.common.DefaultEvaluationContext`, `org.keycloak.authorization.model.Scope`, `org.keycloak.models.RealmModel`, `org.keycloak.representations.AccessToken`, the static import `org.keycloak.services.resources.admin.permissions.AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE`, and the private method `getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken)` (plus the `Map`, `Collection`, `List` transitive uses it drags in) are not referenced anywhere in the file. false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Event listener feature-flag mismatch causes UnsupportedOperationException when both V1 and V2 FGAP are enabled

The event listener body is wrapped in `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))`, but inside it calls `management(...)` which dispatches to MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled. With the new `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` override, that path returns `ClientPermissionsV2`, whose `setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean)` now throws `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`. Before this PR, `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` inherited V1's implementation and the call worked. As a result, in a realm where both `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` and `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` are enabled, any `ClientRemovedEvent` (or `RoleRemovedEvent`/`GroupRemovedEvent` whose management path is also impacted) will raise `UnsupportedOperationException`. The check should be either `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ && !ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2`, or the calls into the V2 evaluator should be guarded so that the unsupported operation is not invoked when V2 is in effect.

No test exercises the MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope for clients

The new `ClientPermissionsV2.canMapClientScopeRoles(ClientModel)` (and its corresponding schema scope `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE`) is declared on the interface and implemented, but `PermissionClientTest` does not contain a test case that grants `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE` and verifies the associated behavior is allowed, nor a negative case. Only `MAP_ROLES` and `MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE` are exercised through `testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient`. A dedicated test should be added so the new scope is covered by the test suite.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exit code 4 silently reassigned, breaking scripts that check for recreate upgrade

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was 4 and is now 3; the new FEATURE_DISABLED constant takes the previous value of 4. Any consumer that was scripting against `update-compatibility check` and matching exit code 4 to detect a recreate-upgrade outcome will now silently treat a 'feature disabled' failure as a recreate upgrade. The error messages differ but the exit code, which is what the docs recommend scripts rely on ('they should rely only on the exit code of the `check` command'), has changed. Even for a preview feature this is a contract break worth calling out in the release notes; alternatively, reserve a new code (e.g., 5) for FEATURE_DISABLED and leave RECREATE at 4 to preserve backward compatibility.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
Exit code 4 description is misleading

The exit-code table describes code 4 as 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible. The feature `rolling-updates` is disabled.', but in this case the command does not actually determine whether a rolling upgrade is possible — `AbstractUpdatesCommand.printFeatureDisabled()` short-circuits the command and prints 'Unable to use this command. The preview feature `rolling-updates` is not enabled.' before any compatibility analysis. The wording should make it clear that the command itself could not run (e.g., 'The command cannot run. The feature `rolling-updates` is disabled.') rather than implying a compatibility verdict was reached.

No coverage for UpdateCompatibilityCheck with feature disabled

`testFeatureNotEnabled` only exercises `update-compatibility metadata` when the feature is disabled. `UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run()` has the same feature gate added (see quarkus/runtime/.../UpdateCompatibilityCheck.java) and is the more important subcommand for users (per docs: 'they should rely only on the exit code of the `check` command'). A symmetric test launching `update-compatibility check` without `--features=rolling-updates` and asserting both the error message and exit code 4 is needed to prevent regressions in the check subcommand.

testFeatureNotEnabled does not assert exit code 4

The test only verifies the stderr error message produced by `printFeatureDisabled()`, but the contract introduced by this PR is also that the command exits with CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED (4). The PR description and the docs explicitly state 'they should rely only on the exit code of the `check` command', so the test for the new exit code should assert `cliResult.exitCode() == 4` (and ideally `assertExitCode`-style). Without it, an implementation that returned exit code 0 (or any other value) while still printing the message would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
V2 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses resource UUID instead of group name

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() (line 122), the lambda iterates over resources of type "Groups" and calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) while also adding groupResource.getId() to the granted set. groupResource.getId() is the resource's internal UUID (a system-generated identifier), but the contract of getGroupIdsWithViewPermission requires group IDs (GroupModel.getId()), which are stored as the resource's name. Two consequences follow: (1) hasPermission does findByName(server, groupId) with the resource UUID, so per-group resources (which are named with the group ID) are never matched and the code always falls through to the all-groups resource check. As a result per-group V2 permissions are effectively ignored when computing the visible-group set. (2) The set returned to callers contains resource UUIDs, not group IDs, so downstream consumers (UsersResource.searchForUser / getUsersCount and BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser) end up storing nonsense values in session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, ...) and passing them to user search/count queries, producing wrong results and silent functional regressions whenever an admin has any level of V2 group VIEW_MEMBERS / MANAGE_MEMBERS permission. The fix should be hasPermission(groupResource.getName(), ...) and granted.add(groupResource.getName()). Existing GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest cases do not exercise the all-groups-level permission path, so they do not detect this regression.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

false_positives.candidate:
JavaDoc says getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns a Stream

The JavaDoc on GroupPermissionEvaluator.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (added in this PR, line 144-147) reads "@return Stream of IDs of groups with view permission." but the declared return type (and the implementations in both GroupPermissions and GroupPermissionsV2) is Set<String>. Either the wording "Stream of IDs" is a leftover that should be "Set of IDs", or the return type was meant to be a stream. This is the only contract documentation of a method that several other files depend on, so it should be accurate.

Potential NPE when all-groups resource cannot be resolved

In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission (lines 144-150), when groupId-specific lookup returns null the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...).getResourceTypeResource can return null (e.g. when supportsAuthorizationSchema is false, the resourceType is unknown, or the all-groups resource was never created). That null value is then passed unchecked to policyStore.findByResource(server, resource), which on the common JPA/in-memory store implementations will NPE. A simple null check on the result of getResourceTypeResource, or treating a null return as "no all-groups resource -> no permission", would make the code robust.

HTML_TAGS regex is case-sensitive and misses uppercase tags `Pattern HTML_TAGS = Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>");` only matches lower-case tag names. Real-world translations can use mixed-case or upper-case tags (e.g., `

Locale-matching regex includes unintended characters due to misplaced `-`

The pattern `"_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties"` contains the character class `[a-zA-Z-_]`. Java's regex interprets the `-` between `Z` and `_` as a range, so the class actually matches `a-z`, `A-Z`, `[`, `\\`, `]`, `^`, `_`. For typical locale codes (`de`, `zh_CN`, etc.) this happens to work, but a malformed locale segment could be accepted. Move the `-` to the end of the class to make it literal: `_[a-zA-Z_-]*\\.properties`.

PolicyFactory instances are not static final

They are immutable and shared between instances, so they should be `private static final`. This avoids rebuilding the OWASP policies for every file checked and makes the intent explicit.

When the English counterpart file (computed via `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community","resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties","_en.properties")`) does not exist, the catch block wraps the `FileNotFoundException` as `new RuntimeException("unable to read file " + englishFile, e)`. true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor requireNonNull checks wrong variable for rawTokenId

The fourth argument of the constructor is `String rawTokenId`, but the validation reads `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");`. The check uses `grantType` (already validated on the previous line) and so cannot fail. As a result `rawTokenId` is never validated and a null raw token id silently passes the constructor and is later encoded into the produced token id. It should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted logic and wrong substring range; does not actually verify the grant shortcut

The body asserts: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false; return isUUID().matches(items[1]);`. Two defects combine to make the filter useless:
1) The negation is missing - the substring must equal the expected shortcut for the match to succeed, but the code rejects matches instead.
2) The indices are wrong - the grant-type shortcut occupies positions 4-5 of the prefix (session[0..1], token[2..3], grant[4..5]), so extracting `substring(3, 5)` returns the second character of the token-type shortcut and the first character of the grant shortcut (`ta` for `onrtac`), never the two-char grant shortcut the test expects.

Concretely, for `AuthorizationCodeGrantTypeFactory.GRANT_SHORTCUT = "ac"`, the encoded prefix `onrtac` produces substring `"ta"`, which never equals `"ac"`, so the test falls through to the UUID check and the matcher matches every well-formed id regardless of grant type. For refresh tokens the substring `(online/offline, regular, refresh)` becomes `"rt"`, which DOES equal the expected shortcut and incorrectly FAILS the match. Fix to `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Converting getShouldUseLightweightToken from instance method to public static is a behavioral break for subclasses

`getShouldUseLightweightToken` was previously a package-private instance method. The change turns it into `public static boolean getShouldUseLightweightToken(...)`. Any custom subclass outside the tree (or within) that overrode this method to influence which token type is chosen will silently stop being called - static methods are not dispatched virtually, and their overrides no longer compile cleanly. The PR description does not call this out as an API/SPI change. If the method is meant to be part of an extension contract it should be made `public` only while staying an instance method (or factored into a separate strategy class).

No null check on getShortcut() before using shortcut as map key and in token id encoding

`getShortcutByGrantType` invokes `factory.getShortcut()` and uses the result as both a map key (`grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)`) and as part of the produced token id (`+ grantShort +` in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId`). The interface contract `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` does not forbid null. A custom or future factory returning null would either corrupt the `grantsByShortcuts` map (ConcurrentHashMap rejects null keys, throwing NullPointerException) or cause `encodeTokenId` to concatenate a null piece into the encoded token id (also raising NPE). Add a null-check or document that implementations must return a non-null 2-character shortcut.

Pair of map updates not atomic; transient inconsistency possible under concurrent refresh

`getShortcutByGrantType` performs `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType); grantsToShortcuts.put(grantType, shortcut);` as two separate operations. Concurrent callers loading a brand new grant type can leave the cache in a window where one direction (shortcut -> grant type) is populated and the other (grant type -> shortcut) is not yet visible. A concurrent reader doing the opposite lookup at that moment will not find the entry and may either retry (incurring an extra `getProviderFactoriesStream` enumeration) or - in the `encodeTokenId` path - throw IllegalStateException("Cannot encode token with unknown grantType") despite the grant being known moments later. Although very unlikely in practice, the two maps are mutated independently under contention; an `AtomicReference<Map<...>>` swap or populating both into temporary maps and then performing atomic `putAll` would be safer.

SpI is marked internal but the PR description advertises extensibility for custom encodings

`TokenContextEncoderSpi.isInternal()` returns `true`, meaning no custom `TokenContextEncoderProviderFactory` implementations can be registered through the normal Spi lookup. The PR description states the SpI was introduced so that "someone (can) introduce his own provider ... and eventually encode some more info or encode stuff in the different way etc." These two statements are mutually exclusive: if the SpI is internal, downstream implementations cannot plug in. Either the SpI should be public (and `isInternal()` should return `false`), or the PR description should be corrected and the indirection justified purely for testability - in which case the `TokenContextEncoderProvider`/`...Factory` types could live in a single class without an SpI.

grantType field is cached from form params at construction but not refreshed when setFormParams is called later

Dead method `_create_process_for_shard` is never invoked

The method `_create_process_for_shard` (lines 127-132) is defined but never called anywhere in the file or by any caller. The corresponding `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) is the one used by `_create_processes` and `_ensure_processes_alive`. The check is `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS:` and the counter is incremented after the check. So the counter can take the values 0..10 with the check still False, then 11 with the check True. That means the consumer will restart an unhealthy flusher process 11 times before crashing, not 10 as the constant name and original semantics imply. Either rename the constant, change the check to `>=`, or move the increment before the check.

`process_restarts` counter never resets, so a long-running consumer is doomed by transient crashes

`self.process_restarts[process_index]` is initialized to 0 in `__init__` and only ever incremented in `_ensure_processes_alive`; it is never reset on successful operation. For a long-lived consumer that is rebalanced occasionally and where the SpanFlusher is reconstructed, this is bounded, but the per-process restart counter is shared across the lifetime of the SpanFlusher object. A single flusher that crashes 11 times over the course of days for transient reasons (deploys, brief OOM kills, broker hiccups) will permanently take down the consumer with no path to recovery short of a full restart. Consider resetting the counter once the process has been healthy for a sustained period.

`process_restarts` is incremented before the restart attempt, so failed restarts consume the budget

The order in `_ensure_processes_alive` is: check `> MAX`, increment, then `process.kill()` and `_create_process_for_shards(...)`. If `_create_process_for_shards` raises (e.g., OS resource exhaustion, pickling error), the counter has already been incremented and the next health check will be one step closer to crashing the consumer despite no successful restart ever having occurred. Move the increment to after a successful recreation, or wrap the restart in try/except and only increment on success.

Old flusher process is not joined before spawning its replacement

`_ensure_processes_alive` calls `process.kill()` and then immediately calls `_create_process_for_shards`, which spawns a new `SpawnProcess` and stores it in `self.processes[process_index]`. `kill()` only sends SIGKILL; it does not wait for the OS to actually reap the process. Until the old process is reaped it can still be inside its main loop, still flushing segments from Redis and still mutating the shared `process_healthy_since` / `process_backpressure_since` `Value`s. Once the new process is up, both processes will flush the same shards concurrently, producing duplicate Kafka payloads on `BUFFERED_SEGMENTS` (idempotency assumptions in downstream consumers are likely broken) and racing on the shared `Value`s. Call `process.join(timeout)` (with a short timeout) before spawning the replacement, or use `process.terminate()` followed by `join()` to give it a chance to exit cleanly first.

Additionally, with `num_processes = 0`, the subsequent `for i, shard in enumerate(...): process_index = i % 0` would raise ZeroDivisionError — there is no input validation guarding this.

The updated docstring states 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing', but the constructor takes `max_processes` and defaults it to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. A consumer configured with `--flusher-processes=2` and four shards will create 2 processes, each handling 2 shards. The docstring is therefore misleading; describe the actual semantics (e.g., 'creates up to `max_processes` worker processes, each handling one or more Redis shards').

The new test only verifies that `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes == 2`, `num_processes == 2`, and that 4 shards are distributed. true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

Django QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.') when the start of a slice is negative (django/db/models/query.py). The in-code comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is therefore false. Because Cursor.from_string parses `int(bits[1])` without clamping, and the endpoint gates this branch on superuser/global-access + the query param `optimized_pagination=true`, any such user can craft a cursor with a negative offset and crash the audit log endpoint with a 500 (AssertionError, not a BadPaginationError). The intended 'high-performance bidirectional pagination' feature is unreachable in any working form.

The endpoint's permission_classes (OrganizationAuditPermission) and the query filter on `organization_id` already apply to both code paths identically, so the claim is both misleading and irrelevant to the new behavior. A reviewer relying on this comment to evaluate risk would be misled about the actual attack surface.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is an almost-verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result (lines 136-215), differing only in the extra branch that allows a negative start_offset. This duplication means any future fix, security patch, or bug fix applied to BasePaginator.get_result will silently not apply to the new paginator. Given the new class is only ever selected from one endpoint and one branch, the simpler and safer design is to add an `enable_advanced_features` flag on BasePaginator (or a small subclass that only overrides the slicing step), rather than copy the full state machine including cursor building, prev-page filtering, and post_query_filter handling.

The diff replaces `stop = offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset; stop = start_offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. For any non-negative offset (the normal case) `max(0, offset) == offset`, so this is functionally identical to the prior code; the comment 'For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning' therefore misrepresents a no-op as a performance optimization. For prev cursors with a negative offset the behavior is also unchanged (still crashes in Django; see the related critical finding). Either remove the misleading comment or implement the actual optimization.

Comment suggests new behavior that the code does not add

The Cursor.__init__ change is comment-only: `self.offset = int(offset)` already accepted negative integers before this PR. The new comment 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios. This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets' implies the constructor was modified to permit this, but `int(offset)` was unchanged. This is misleading documentation in a security-sensitive area; reviewers and future maintainers may infer that negative offsets are officially supported when in fact the only consumer (OptimizedCursorPaginator) is broken and no other cursor parsing path validates bounds.

'authorized administrators' mislabels org:global_access

The variable is named `enable_advanced` and the comment says 'for authorized administrators', but the condition is `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. `has_global_access` corresponds to the `org:global_access` scope, which is granted to Sentry employees (staff) for cross-org support, not to organization administrators. Conflating the two is a documentation/UX defect: org owners/admins will not see this code path even if they set `optimized_pagination=true`, while Sentry staff can. The branch's purpose should be described accurately (e.g. 'enable for Sentry staff and superusers') and, if intended for staff, the flag should probably not be exposed at all to non-staff.

New query parameter and paginator branch have no tests

The diff introduces a new query parameter `optimized_pagination`, a new permission-derived branch, and a new paginator class (OptimizedCursorPaginator) with non-trivial behavior (negative offsets, a duplicate state machine, and a feature flag). The PR does not modify or add any tests in the diff (no files under tests/ are listed). true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer serializes per key — duplicate indexes possible

The previous version held `b.cacheMu` for the entire BuildIndex call, so concurrent calls for the same key were serialized and the cached index was consistent. The new version only locks when assigning `b.cache[key] = idx`. Two concurrent calls to `BuildIndex` for the same `NamespacedResource` (for example, two simultaneous `Search` requests that both find the cache empty via `getOrCreateIndex`, or the init goroutine racing with an incoming search) will both:
  1. Open separate bleve indexes (file or memory),
  2. Run the builder to write all documents,
  3. Flush,
  4. Race to write `b.cache[key]` — last writer wins, the loser's index is orphaned in memory and the work is wasted.
The PR description frames this as "finer grain locking", but the same-key duplication problem is exactly the TODO called out in `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` ("We want to block while building the index and return the same index for the key … simple mutex not great … we don't want to block while anything in building, just the same key"). A per-key lock (e.g. a `sync.Map` of in-progress builds, or a sharded mutex keyed by `NamespacedResource`) is needed to actually fix the duplicate-build race while keeping different-key concurrency.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same race condition in `BuildIndex` described in the golden comment: moving `b.cacheMu` to only guard the final cache assignment allows concurrent goroutines to redundantly build the same index for the same key.

Previously the same errors would surface on the first RPC and the constructor returned quickly.
This breaks any caller that expected the constructor to be cheap (tests, callers that wire up dependencies lazily, callers that want to surface a degraded server, callers that explicitly rely on `server.Init` being invoked separately). false_positives.candidate:
Failed messages are silently lost on processing exception

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, the `finally` clause unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` regardless of whether `result_processor` raised. The exception is caught and logged by the inner `except Exception`, but the offset is still marked complete, then committed to Kafka by the commit loop. The message is then gone and will not be retried on restart. This contradicts the strategy's docstring which promises "Only commits offsets after successful processing" and is a serious data integrity issue (e.g., missed uptime check results, missed monitor check-ins). Either the complete_offset must be conditional on success (e.g., a success flag set in the try), or failed messages must be routed to a DLQ. The existing batched-parallel path uses ThreadPoolExecutor.submit which silently captures exceptions, so it has the same data-loss pattern; this PR replicates and deepens the problem for the new mode.

hash() randomization breaks ordering guarantee across restarts

`FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` returns `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). After any restart or new worker process, the same group_key can map to a different queue, violating the documented "Items for the same group are processed in order" guarantee. Example: if the consumer dies after submitting offset N to queue 5 and is restarted, offset N+1 for the same group may be hashed to queue 7 and processed in parallel/independently from any later retry of offset N, breaking in-order processing. Use a stable, cross-process hash like `int(hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)` (or `hashlib.sha256(...)`) instead of `hash()`.

Shutdown ordering can cause workers to exit before draining queues

In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`, `worker.shutdown = True` is set on all workers BEFORE `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called on each queue. The worker loop is `while not self.shutdown: try: work_queue.get() ...`, so a worker that just finished processing one item and is returning to the top of the loop will observe `self.shutdown == True` and exit without ever pulling the next item from its queue. Because the workers have already exited by the time `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` runs, the items left in each queue are never drained and are silently discarded (only re-read from Kafka on next start, if not yet committed). The `worker.shutdown = True` step is also redundant: `q.shutdown()` is sufficient to terminate the workers via the `queue.ShutDown` exception. Remove the `worker.shutdown = True` loop (or move it after the join), so that `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` can actually drain pending items.

This is silent data loss: spans are permanently removed from the segment, no metric is incremented, no log is emitted, and the segment will be flushed incomplete with no way for operators to detect the loss. false_positives.candidate:
_is_error_focused_query uses naive substring matching that yields wrong upsampling decisions

The check `"event.type:error" in query` is a raw substring test on the lowercase query string. As a result it returns True (and therefore triggers error upsampling on the discover dataset) in cases where the query is actually not error-focused, e.g.:

- Negated clauses: `!event.type:error` still contains the substring `event.type:error`.
- Compound queries mixing transactions and errors: `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, `event.type:error something else`, etc.
- Look-alike values: `event.type:errors`, `event.type:error_handled`, any custom tag named `event.type:error*`.

When upsampling is applied in any of these cases, `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (= `sum(sample_weight)`) but the result set includes rows without `sample_weight` (transactions, non-error events), so the returned counts are mathematically wrong and silently inflated/deflated. The docstring claims this check "errs on the side of caution" — in reality it is more permissive than just `event.type:error`. The function should parse the query and require an un-negated, standalone `event.type:error` predicate.

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is added with a docstring that explicitly says it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency across the system", but nothing in the PR (or in any of the modified files) calls it. The 60-second cache in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` therefore becomes stale any time `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is updated: projects added to the allowlist will not be upsampled for up to 60s, and projects removed will continue to be upsampled (returning inflated counts) for up to 60s. This is a correctness hazard for an opt-in metric that drives billing/usage reporting numbers. Either wire up the invalidation in the option-change signal handler or drop the cache and accept the option lookup cost.

upsampled_count SnQLFunction is only registered on the discover dataset but is also injected into errors-dataset queries

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True for the `errors` dataset unconditionally, and the endpoint rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count()` whenever that check passes. The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is, however, only registered on the discover dataset's function map in this PR. So a top-events or non-RPC query routed to the `errors` dataset (which is in the dataset whitelist at lines ~172-188 of `organization_events_stats.py`) will be sent down with a `upsampled_count()` aggregate that the errors dataset's function_converter does not know about, causing a query build/runtime error at request time. If upsampling is meant to work on `errors` as well, register the SnQLFunction on that dataset too; otherwise gate the rewrite so it only applies when the scoped dataset is `discover`.

transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling ignores aliased count()

The transformer compares `column_lower == "count()"` exactly, so any column expression that contains `count()` but is not literally that string is left untouched. In practice that includes:

- Aliased forms: `count() as my_count`, `count() AS count`.
- Annotated forms: `count()` followed by other tokens, e.g. `count(), other_col` (already split into separate items so OK), but also `count(error_count)` if it ever appears bare.
- Aggregations wrapped by other functions: `topK(1)(count())`.

The result is that for the same query, some y-axes are upsampled and others are not, mixing weighted and unweighted counts in the same response and producing nonsense totals / charts in the dashboard. The match should be against the leading aggregate token rather than the whole trimmed string.

_are_all_projects_error_upsampled does not validate the allowlist option type

`options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", [])` is used directly with `project_id in allowlist`. If the option is ever misconfigured (set to a string, tuple, generator, etc.), `in` falls back to iteration/substring semantics — for a string allowlist, `123 in "1234"` returns True and arbitrary project IDs will be considered allowlisted, silently enabling upsampling (and inflated counts) for the wrong tenants. There is no schema/option validator in this PR and no isinstance(list)/set coercion in the consumer. Coerce `allowlist` to a `set` (and assert the type) before the membership check.

Both `try: ... except Exception: pass` blocks around the `contexts.error_sampling` lookup and the `float(...)` conversion in `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` silently discard every error. Because this runs on every `store_event` call in tests (and could be wired into production ingestion), any structural change to the event dict (renamed contexts, different nesting, AttributeError on a non-dict `contexts`, etc.) will fail silently and leave `sample_rate` unset with no log/raise. The actual substring check is more permissive than just `event.type:error` (it also matches `!event.type:error`, `event.type:errors`, compound OR queries with transactions), and the sample_weight assumption is not enforced anywhere visible in this PR. These comments will mislead future maintainers into trusting the function's output. Either tighten the implementation to match the comments or update the comments to describe the real behavior.

As a result, every concurrent goroutine that observes a nil cache in the fast path will acquire the write lock in turn and each redundantly re-read the manifest file and re-parse the JSON. This is the classic double-checked-locking pitfall: the fast-path RLock/RUnlock check at lines 41-43 is not mirrored inside the Lock-held critical section. At Grafana startup, where many HTTP handlers can call this function concurrently, this causes N redundant file reads and JSON decodes instead of one. The fix is to add a re-check inside the write-lock critical section, e.g. by inserting `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` on line 48.

The corresponding JS (`Discourse.ajax('/admin/groups/' + this.get('id') + '/members.json', ...)`) matches those URLs, so the param that holds the group id is `params[:id]`. However, both new actions read the group with `Group.find(params.require(:group_id).to_i)` (line 66 for add_members, line 85 for remove_member). Because `params[:group_id]` is never populated by the router, every real PUT/DELETE from the admin UI will raise `ActionController::ParameterMissing` and the add/remove member functionality will be completely broken in production. The controller specs pass because RSpec controller specs bypass routing and inject `group_id:` directly into the params hash, which is exactly the test gap that hides this bug. Either change the actions to read `params[:id]`/`params.require(:id)`, or add a `:group_id` segment to the routes.

`usernames.split(",").each do |username| ... User.find_by_username(username)` is called verbatim on each substring. If the user-selector ever produces a name with surrounding whitespace (e.g. `"alice , bob"` or stray trailing whitespace from an autocomplete suggestion), `User.find_by_username(" alice ")` returns nil and the entry is silently dropped — the request still returns `success_json`, the admin sees "added" and no user was actually added. Similar trimming is performed in other parts of the app (e.g. user creation) and would be expected here.

On failure the controller does `var message = $.parseJSON(e.responseText).errors;`. true_positives.matched_candidate:

If the save fails (e.g. DB connection blip, lock timeout, race causing a stale `match_count` that triggers a future validation), ActiveRecord raises and the user sees a generic 500 instead of a clean signup error. `email_in_restriction_setting?` only does `setting.gsub('.', '\.')` before building `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)`. The whitelist/blacklist values are admin-controlled site settings that may contain `|`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `+`, `*`, `?`, `^`, `$`, `\`. A value like `gmail.com|mail.ru` would match `@gmail.com` *or* `@mail.ru` (the first `|` makes `mail.ru` a separate alternative of the whole group, not a literal). Also, because the pattern is `@(...)` with no anchors, a blacklist value of `mail.ru` already matches `user@mail.ru.example.com`. Escape all regex metacharacters and anchor the match (e.g. require the domain to end at a non-word character or end of string) so neither false positives nor ReDoS-via-admin-setting is possible.

A user can trivially bypass a block by signing up with `BAD@spamclub.com`, `bad@spamclub.com ` (trailing space), etc., and the same bypass defeats the admin's intent when they later look up rows in `blocked_emails`. false_positives.candidate:

`record.match_count += 1; record.save` is a read-modify-write on a single row with no row lock. Under any concurrent signups for the same blocked address (and Discourse runs Puma/clustered workers), two callers can both read e.g. `match_count = 5`, both bump to 6, and both persist 6 — losing one increment. The same problem affects `last_match_at`. Use an atomic SQL update, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(["match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", Time.zone.now])`, so the counter cannot be lost.

Referer-based authorization is fragile and bypassable

`ensure_embeddable` only checks `URI(request.referer || '').host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The Referer header is freely spoofable in many environments (browsers with privacy extensions, server-side fetchers, embedded webviews, curl), it can be wholly absent (in which case the empty string still passes URI parsing and compares mismatched, denying the request), and the comparison is a plain string match that ignores ports/scheme. The job requires `email/sender` but never references it (and TopicRetriever does not either). Remove the unused dependency to avoid loading unnecessary code paths and to prevent surprising coupling when email/Sender changes.

The spec only exercises the gated path through `retrieve` and asserts that `perform_retrieve` is or isn't called. 5 downsize iterations are mathematically insufficient for the feature to work

Each pass uses `"80%"` dimensions, which shrinks image area to 0.8² = 0.64 of the original, so the file size drops by roughly 36% per iteration. After 5 iterations the file is approximately 0.64⁵ ≈ 33% of the original. With the default `max_image_size_kb` of 10MB, any source image above ~30MB cannot be brought under the limit in 5 passes; for example a 50MB image ends up at ~16MB and a 100MB image at ~33MB. The `while` loop then exits and `Upload.create_for` is invoked with an oversized file, so the 'auto-downsize' feature silently fails for any but moderately large images. Either the iteration count must scale with the initial size, the reduction factor must be more aggressive, or the loop should compute the required scale per iteration and pass it to `OptimizedImage.downsize`.

The 413 branch of `displayErrorForUpload` previously displayed `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` in the user-facing `file_too_large` error. It now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024`, so the size quoted in the error dialog no longer matches the actual configured `max_image_size_kb`. Users will see '10MB' even when the real limit is 2MB or 50MB, leading to confusing UX after any admin change to the site setting.

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` reads from and writes to the same path. If the convert/gifsicle invocation fails (corrupt input, OOM, signal, bad permissions), ImageMagick may truncate or zero out the file before erroring, and the loop never checks the return value (`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns true/false), so the next iteration or the subsequent `Upload.create_for` will run on a corrupted/empty file. The fix is to write to a separate temp path, verify the result, then atomically rename, and to break out of the loop when downsize reports failure rather than blindly iterating again.

Date-override day match is compared in UTC, not organizer tz

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` compares two UTC-formatted dates. The date override is a calendar day in the organizer's timezone, and `slotStartTime` is in UTC. Around the day boundary (e.g. override on 2024-01-01 IST = 2023-12-31 18:30 UTC …) a slot on the correct local day can be compared against the wrong UTC date and the override will be silently ignored. Use the organizer's timezone for both sides of the comparison (e.g. `dayjs.tz(slotStartTime, organizerTimeZone).format(...)`).

Override boundary check is strict, missing same-instant starts

`slotStartTime.isAfter(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` is strict: a slot whose start equals the override end is not filtered, and slots that straddle the override end (e.g. override 14:00–18:00, slot 17:30–18:30) are also not filtered because there is no check that the slot end is within the override. The check should also require `slotStartTime` not to be after `date.end` (use `isSameOrAfter` or also verify the slot end) and the same boundary issue applies to `date.start` (a slot that begins before the override starts but ends inside it slips through).

At minimum, the handler should use an advisory lock keyed on the workflow step or use an idempotent update (`update where retryCount = <stale value>`) to make the increment safe.

false_positives.candidate:
Webhook handler accepts any HTTP method

The handler does not check `req.method` before processing. Combined with no CSRF protection and a single shared secret, this lets an attacker who learns the secret invoke the endpoint via GET (which Next.js does not JSON-parse by default, so `reqBody = z.parse(undefined)` will throw a 500), or submit via PUT/DELETE which could also expose side effects. The endpoint should explicitly require POST and reject other methods with 405.

Unprotected JSON.parse after decrypt can crash the request

`symmetricDecrypt` returns the raw decrypted bytes and the result is fed directly into `JSON.parse` with no try/catch. If the symmetric decrypt throws (bad key, tampered ciphertext, wrong padding) or the plaintext is not valid JSON, the handler crashes with an uncaught exception and returns a generic 500 instead of a 4xx. This also means the webhook secret check, user existence check, etc. cannot return a proper error. The decrypt and parse should be wrapped, and the result should be validated as an object before being assigned to `key`.

findFirst-then-create is racy and can duplicate credentials

The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ userId, appId })` followed by `update` or `create` with no transaction. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same (userId, appId) can both observe no existing credential and both insert, leaving two `Credential` rows that downstream code (which does `findFirst` in e.g. office365video callback) cannot reliably deduplicate. Use `prisma.credential.upsert` with a unique compound key, or wrap the read/write in a transaction with appropriate isolation.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality

The webhook secret is compared with `!==`. Although the secret is shared and not user-derived, attackers can in principle exploit timing differences to recover the secret byte by byte. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` against buffers of equal length (after a length check) to close this side channel.

Credential type sourced from app metadata, not the request

When creating a credential, the code uses `appMetadata.type` for `type` while the existing callbacks elsewhere in the codebase store values like `"google_calendar"`, `"hubspot_other_calendar"`, `"office365_video"`, etc. If `appStoreMetadata`'s `type` differs from the conventional string used elsewhere for the same app (or if the DB `app` row's slug does not match the metadata entry's slug), the new credential's `type` column will not match what CalendarService implementations later filter on, causing the freshly synced credential to be ignored.

Outgoing credential-sync POST has no authentication

When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, this function POSTs `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` to the configured endpoint with no auth header. The receiving endpoint cannot verify the request came from this Cal.com instance, and a network attacker (or anyone who knows the endpoint URL) can impersonate arbitrary Cal.com users to obtain refreshed tokens. The same `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (and matching header name) that the incoming webhook requires should be sent on this outgoing request.

Salesforce getClient refreshes the OAuth token on every instantiation

`getClient` now unconditionally POSTs to the Salesforce token endpoint on every call, then writes the response to the DB. Previously Salesforce never did a refresh in this code path; every connection was constructed from the stored `credentialKey`. With the new code each `CalendarService` construction (and therefore each event create/update/getAvailability cycle that goes through the manager) makes an extra network round trip and a DB write. Add an expiry check before refreshing, matching the patterns used by googlecalendar / hubspot / webex.

`export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` evaluates to the encryption-key string when both env vars are set, or to `undefined`/`""` otherwise. Call sites use it in `if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)` (truthy check), which works in practice, but it is documented/used as a boolean flag. Coerce explicitly: `Boolean(process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY)` so the type matches usage and an empty-string secret cannot accidentally enable sharing.

JSON.parse on req.query.state has no error handling

`JSON.parse(req.query.state)` will throw a SyntaxError if the state parameter is not valid JSON, turning the OAuth `add` endpoint into a 500. This code path is exercised only on path renames in this PR, but the file was moved and is part of the changed set; a `try`/`catch` returning `undefined` (matching the early-return for non-string state) would be safer. Same issue in `decodeOAuthState.ts`.

The endpoint accepts encrypted credentials that fully overwrite a user's third-party OAuth tokens (potentially including refresh tokens) for any app, gated only by a single shared secret. The PR description acknowledges no tests were added. At minimum: tests for wrong/missing secret (403), unknown user (404), unknown app (404), invalid encrypted payload (4xx, not 500), missing/short encryption key, and concurrent writes for the same (userId, appId) should exist before merge.

Combined with the dialog's unrestricted email entry, any original invitee can inject any third-party email into the booking, getting them full calendar details, organizer info, other attendees, and a meeting invitation without the organizer's consent. The organizer should normally be the only one (plus team admins/owners) permitted to add guests. This is a serious privacy/access-control issue.

The flow is: `prisma.booking.update` (commits new attendees) -> `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` -> `sendAddGuestsEmails` (wrapped only in a `console.log` on error). If `updateCalendarAttendees` throws (e.g., bad credentials, video provider error), the guests remain in the database but never receive an invite; the caller sees a TRPC error and may retry, creating duplicates. An empty `name` will render as a blank attendee in the UI (booking list, emails, calendar) and confuses no-show/dropdown flows. `value.map((field, index) => <li key={index}>...)`. When a user removes an item in the middle of the list, every input after it is re-bound to the wrong value (because React reuses the DOM and state by index). An attacker who already has the user's password can therefore brute-force the ten 10-hex-char backup codes at full speed (only bcrypt on the password limits them, and that throttling is per user, not per attempt). The endpoint also never marks the consumed code, so even a correct guess leaves the rest usable. Add a rate limit per (userId, IP) and reuse the atomic consumption pattern from the credentials authorize flow.

All-codes-exhausted state is indistinguishable from a typo

When a user has consumed every backup code, `backupCodes` is `[null, null, ..., null]`. `user.backupCodes` is still a non-empty encrypted string, so the `if (!user.backupCodes) throw MissingBackupCodes` guard never fires. The user instead gets `IncorrectBackupCode` on every attempt, with no way to tell that they've actually run out of codes. After decrypt+parse, detect the case where every element is null/missing and throw `MissingBackupCodes` (or a new dedicated error) so the UI can surface a clear message and the user knows to re-enable 2FA and regenerate codes.

Backup-code login and disable paths are not end-to-end tested

The new e2e additions only exercise the backup-codes dialog (download/copy/close) after enabling 2FA. The two security-critical paths this PR introduces — logging in via backup code from `apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx` (`twoFactorLostAccess` flow) and disabling 2FA via the 'Lost access' path in `DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx` — have no test at all. The PR description itself acknowledges 'I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective'. For an authentication feature, both the happy path and the wrong-code / exhausted-code negative paths must be covered, and the consumed-once invariant should be asserted (e.g. login with the same code twice, second attempt must fail).

resetState leaves isSubmitting, backupCodes, secret and dataUri in place

`resetState()` only clears `password`, `errorMessage`, and `step`. It does not reset `isSubmitting`, `backupCodes`, `backupCodesUrl` (blob URL — see separate finding), `dataUri`, or `secret`. If the modal is closed and reopened, the next 'Continue' button can stay disabled (because `isSubmitting` may still be true from a previous round), and the stale `secret` / `dataUri` could be displayed against a brand-new secret if the user races the step transitions. Reset all transient state and revoke any pending blob URL inside `resetState`.

body.backupCodes assumed to be present and a string array

Right after `await response.json()`, the code does `body.backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode)` with no guard. If the server ever returns an error body that lacks `backupCodes`, or returns it under a different key, or with non-string elements, the page crashes mid-setup and `setIsSubmitting(false)` runs but the user is left on a broken step. Validate the shape (Array.isArray and every element is a string) before using it, and fall back to the existing `something_went_wrong` error if it isn't.

false_positives.candidate:
Dead method `_create_process_for_shard` is never invoked

The method `_create_process_for_shard` (lines 127-132) is defined but never called anywhere in the file or by any caller. The corresponding `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) is the one used by `_create_processes` and `_ensure_processes_alive`. Either delete the dead method or wire it up — leaving it in production code is misleading and means future maintainers will assume shard-level restart is supported when it is not.

`MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` allows 11 restarts instead of the 10 the name suggests

The check is `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS:` and the counter is incremented after the check. So the counter can take the values 0..10 with the check still False, then 11 with the check True. That means the consumer will restart an unhealthy flusher process 11 times before crashing, not 10 as the constant name and original semantics imply. Either rename the constant, change the check to `>=`, or move the increment before the check.

`process_restarts` counter never resets, so a long-running consumer is doomed by transient crashes

`self.process_restarts[process_index]` is initialized to 0 in `__init__` and only ever incremented in `_ensure_processes_alive`; it is never reset on successful operation. For a long-lived consumer that is rebalanced occasionally and where the SpanFlusher is reconstructed, this is bounded, but the per-process restart counter is shared across the lifetime of the SpanFlusher object. A single flusher that crashes 11 times over the course of days for transient reasons (deploys, brief OOM kills, broker hiccups) will permanently take down the consumer with no path to recovery short of a full restart. Consider resetting the counter once the process has been healthy for a sustained period.

`process_restarts` is incremented before the restart attempt, so failed restarts consume the budget

The order in `_ensure_processes_alive` is: check `> MAX`, increment, then `process.kill()` and `_create_process_for_shards(...)`. If `_create_process_for_shards` raises (e.g., OS resource exhaustion, pickling error), the counter has already been incremented and the next health check will be one step closer to crashing the consumer despite no successful restart ever having occurred. Move the increment to after a successful recreation, or wrap the restart in try/except and only increment on success.

Old flusher process is not joined before spawning its replacement

`_ensure_processes_alive` calls `process.kill()` and then immediately calls `_create_process_for_shards`, which spawns a new `SpawnProcess` and stores it in `self.processes[process_index]`. `kill()` only sends SIGKILL; it does not wait for the OS to actually reap the process. Until the old process is reaped it can still be inside its main loop, still flushing segments from Redis and still mutating the shared `process_healthy_since` / `process_backpressure_since` `Value`s. Once the new process is up, both processes will flush the same shards concurrently, producing duplicate Kafka payloads on `BUFFERED_SEGMENTS` (idempotency assumptions in downstream consumers are likely broken) and racing on the shared `Value`s. Call `process.join(timeout)` (with a short timeout) before spawning the replacement, or use `process.terminate()` followed by `join()` to give it a chance to exit cleanly first.

`max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` silently treats 0 as None

The `or` falls back to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` whenever `max_processes` is falsy. Passing `max_processes=0` (e.g., to explicitly disable the flusher) will instead spin up a process per shard. Use `if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` so that 0 is honored. Additionally, with `num_processes = 0`, the subsequent `for i, shard in enumerate(...): process_index = i % 0` would raise ZeroDivisionError — there is no input validation guarding this.

Class docstring says 'one process per shard' but the implementation creates up to `max_processes`

The updated docstring states 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing', but the constructor takes `max_processes` and defaults it to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. A consumer configured with `--flusher-processes=2` and four shards will create 2 processes, each handling 2 shards. The docstring is therefore misleading; describe the actual semantics (e.g., 'creates up to `max_processes` worker processes, each handling one or more Redis shards').

`test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts setup, not that flushing actually works

The new test only verifies that `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes == 2`, `num_processes == 2`, and that 4 shards are distributed. It does not submit any spans, so it cannot catch regressions where the per-process buffers route reads to the wrong Redis keys, where the multiprocessing Value objects are misbound, where restart logic corrupts `process_to_shards_map`, or where flushes are silently dropped because a process never sees data assigned to its shards. Extend the test to submit spans to at least two different shards and assert they reach the pipe, ideally with assertions that each process only flushed its assigned shards.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset is negative, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset = cursor.offset (negative). Django QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.') when the start of a slice is negative (django/db/models/query.py). The in-code comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is therefore false. Because Cursor.from_string parses `int(bits[1])` without clamping, and the endpoint gates this branch on superuser/global-access + the query param `optimized_pagination=true`, any such user can craft a cursor with a negative offset and crash the audit log endpoint with a 500 (AssertionError, not a BadPaginationError). The intended 'high-performance bidirectional pagination' feature is unreachable in any working form.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses negative slice offsets on a Django queryset, which Django does not support and which raises an AssertionError.

The comment 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' next to the negative-offset branch implies that negative slicing is gated by some access control. No such check exists: the only gate is `self.enable_advanced_features`, which is set from the endpoint for any superuser or member with `org:global_access`. The endpoint's permission_classes (OrganizationAuditPermission) and the query filter on `organization_id` already apply to both code paths identically, so the claim is both misleading and irrelevant to the new behavior. A reviewer relying on this comment to evaluate risk would be misled about the actual attack surface.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is an almost-verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result (lines 136-215), differing only in the extra branch that allows a negative start_offset. This duplication means any future fix, security patch, or bug fix applied to BasePaginator.get_result will silently not apply to the new paginator. Given the new class is only ever selected from one endpoint and one branch, the simpler and safer design is to add an `enable_advanced_features` flag on BasePaginator (or a small subclass that only overrides the slicing step), rather than copy the full state machine including cursor building, prev-page filtering, and post_query_filter handling.

'Performance optimization' comment describes a no-op change

The diff replaces `stop = offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset; stop = start_offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. For any non-negative offset (the normal case) `max(0, offset) == offset`, so this is functionally identical to the prior code; the comment 'For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning' therefore misrepresents a no-op as a performance optimization. For prev cursors with a negative offset the behavior is also unchanged (still crashes in Django; see the related critical finding). Either remove the misleading comment or implement the actual optimization.

Comment suggests new behavior that the code does not add

The Cursor.__init__ change is comment-only: `self.offset = int(offset)` already accepted negative integers before this PR. The new comment 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios. This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets' implies the constructor was modified to permit this, but `int(offset)` was unchanged. This is misleading documentation in a security-sensitive area; reviewers and future maintainers may infer that negative offsets are officially supported when in fact the only consumer (OptimizedCursorPaginator) is broken and no other cursor parsing path validates bounds.

'authorized administrators' mislabels org:global_access

The variable is named `enable_advanced` and the comment says 'for authorized administrators', but the condition is `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. `has_global_access` corresponds to the `org:global_access` scope, which is granted to Sentry employees (staff) for cross-org support, not to organization administrators. Conflating the two is a documentation/UX defect: org owners/admins will not see this code path even if they set `optimized_pagination=true`, while Sentry staff can. The branch's purpose should be described accurately (e.g. 'enable for Sentry staff and superusers') and, if intended for staff, the flag should probably not be exposed at all to non-staff.

New query parameter and paginator branch have no tests

The diff introduces a new query parameter `optimized_pagination`, a new permission-derived branch, and a new paginator class (OptimizedCursorPaginator) with non-trivial behavior (negative offsets, a duplicate state machine, and a feature flag). The PR does not modify or add any tests in the diff (no files under tests/ are listed). At minimum there should be tests covering: (1) the endpoint dispatches to OptimizedCursorPaginator only when both the flag and the permission gate are set; (2) the standard DateTimePaginator path is used otherwise; (3) cursor encoding/decoding round-trips for the new path; (4) the failure mode for negative offsets (which currently is an uncaught AssertionError, see critical finding). true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer serializes per key — duplicate indexes possible

The previous version held `b.cacheMu` for the entire BuildIndex call, so concurrent calls for the same key were serialized and the cached index was consistent. The new version only locks when assigning `b.cache[key] = idx`. Two concurrent calls to `BuildIndex` for the same `NamespacedResource` (for example, two simultaneous `Search` requests that both find the cache empty via `getOrCreateIndex`, or the init goroutine racing with an incoming search) will both:
  1. Open separate bleve indexes (file or memory),
  2. Run the builder to write all documents,
  3. Flush,
  4. Race to write `b.cache[key]` — last writer wins, the loser's index is orphaned in memory and the work is wasted.
The PR description frames this as "finer grain locking", but the same-key duplication problem is exactly the TODO called out in `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` ("We want to block while building the index and return the same index for the key … simple mutex not great … we don't want to block while anything in building, just the same key"). A per-key lock (e.g. a `sync.Map` of in-progress builds, or a sharded mutex keyed by `NamespacedResource`) is needed to actually fix the duplicate-build race while keeping different-key concurrency.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: narrowing b.cacheMu locking to the final cache assignment allows concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key to duplicate expensive index construction.

Previously the same errors would surface on the first RPC and the constructor returned quickly.
This breaks any caller that expected the constructor to be cheap (tests, callers that wire up dependencies lazily, callers that want to surface a degraded server, callers that explicitly rely on `server.Init` being invoked separately). The PR description itself flags this concern ("Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily? What could this break?") without answering it. Verify all callers of `NewResourceServer` and the SQL `NewBackend` (which now also returns only after `Init` succeeds, since its backend implements the resource LifecycleHooks path) before merging — at minimum, document the contract change on the function and make sure module startup won't now fail outright where it previously degraded.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated once at class definition, not per instance

The field declaration `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` causes `timezone.now()` to be evaluated exactly once when the class body is executed (at module import time), not each time an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. Every instance created in the same process — including those produced by `AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` during inbound webhooks — will share the same `queued` timestamp (the time the module was first imported). For a long-running web server this means `queued` is effectively a process start time, not the time the assignment was queued. The field is part of the serialized payload (`to_dict`/`from_dict`) and is clearly meant to record when the change was queued, so any future logic that relies on it (staleness checks, ordering, debugging) will be wrong. The fix is to use `field(default_factory=lambda: timezone.now())` from `dataclasses`.
