false_positives.candidate:
Failed messages are silently lost on processing exception

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, the `finally` clause unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` regardless of whether `result_processor` raised. The exception is caught and logged by the inner `except Exception`, but the offset is still marked complete, then committed to Kafka by the commit loop. The message is then gone and will not be retried on restart. This contradicts the strategy's docstring which promises "Only commits offsets after successful processing" and is a serious data integrity issue (e.g., missed uptime check results, missed monitor check-ins). Either the complete_offset must be conditional on success (e.g., a success flag set in the try), or failed messages must be routed to a DLQ. The existing batched-parallel path uses ThreadPoolExecutor.submit which silently captures exceptions, so it has the same data-loss pattern; this PR replicates and deepens the problem for the new mode.

hash() randomization breaks ordering guarantee across restarts

`FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` returns `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). After any restart or new worker process, the same group_key can map to a different queue, violating the documented "Items for the same group are processed in order" guarantee. Example: if the consumer dies after submitting offset N to queue 5 and is restarted, offset N+1 for the same group may be hashed to queue 7 and processed in parallel/independently from any later retry of offset N, breaking in-order processing. Use a stable, cross-process hash like `int(hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)` (or `hashlib.sha256(...)`) instead of `hash()`.

Shutdown ordering can cause workers to exit before draining queues

In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`, `worker.shutdown = True` is set on all workers BEFORE `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called on each queue. The worker loop is `while not self.shutdown: try: work_queue.get() ...`, so a worker that just finished processing one item and is returning to the top of the loop will observe `self.shutdown == True` and exit without ever pulling the next item from its queue. Because the workers have already exited by the time `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` runs, the items left in each queue are never drained and are silently discarded (only re-read from Kafka on next start, if not yet committed). The `worker.shutdown = True` step is also redundant: `q.shutdown()` is sufficient to terminate the workers via the `queue.ShutDown` exception. Remove the `worker.shutdown = True` loop (or move it after the join), so that `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` can actually drain pending items.

Cutting the limit to 1000 means 10x more chains (especially long, deep spans trees common in distributed traces with many ancestor pointers) will silently fail to be merged, producing orphaned/incomplete segments flushed on the no-root timeout. The PR description ("Test 2") does not justify this regression.

This is silent data loss: spans are permanently removed from the segment, no metric is incremented, no log is emitted, and the segment will be flushed incomplete with no way for operators to detect the loss. Even the prior Python-side metric `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` is no longer reachable (see buffer.py finding). false_positives.candidate:
_is_error_focused_query uses naive substring matching that yields wrong upsampling decisions

The check `"event.type:error" in query` is a raw substring test on the lowercase query string. As a result it returns True (and therefore triggers error upsampling on the discover dataset) in cases where the query is actually not error-focused, e.g.:

- Negated clauses: `!event.type:error` still contains the substring `event.type:error`.
- Compound queries mixing transactions and errors: `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, `event.type:error something else`, etc.
- Look-alike values: `event.type:errors`, `event.type:error_handled`, any custom tag named `event.type:error*`.

When upsampling is applied in any of these cases, `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (= `sum(sample_weight)`) but the result set includes rows without `sample_weight` (transactions, non-error events), so the returned counts are mathematically wrong and silently inflated/deflated. The docstring claims this check "errs on the side of caution" — in reality it is more permissive than just `event.type:error`. The function should parse the query and require an un-negated, standalone `event.type:error` predicate.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but never called, so the 60s allowlist cache is ungovernable

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is added with a docstring that explicitly says it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency across the system", but nothing in the PR (or in any of the modified files) calls it. The 60-second cache in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` therefore becomes stale any time `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is updated: projects added to the allowlist will not be upsampled for up to 60s, and projects removed will continue to be upsampled (returning inflated counts) for up to 60s. This is a correctness hazard for an opt-in metric that drives billing/usage reporting numbers. Either wire up the invalidation in the option-change signal handler or drop the cache and accept the option lookup cost.

upsampled_count SnQLFunction is only registered on the discover dataset but is also injected into errors-dataset queries

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True for the `errors` dataset unconditionally, and the endpoint rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count()` whenever that check passes. The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is, however, only registered on the discover dataset's function map in this PR. So a top-events or non-RPC query routed to the `errors` dataset (which is in the dataset whitelist at lines ~172-188 of `organization_events_stats.py`) will be sent down with a `upsampled_count()` aggregate that the errors dataset's function_converter does not know about, causing a query build/runtime error at request time. If upsampling is meant to work on `errors` as well, register the SnQLFunction on that dataset too; otherwise gate the rewrite so it only applies when the scoped dataset is `discover`.

transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling ignores aliased count()

The transformer compares `column_lower == "count()"` exactly, so any column expression that contains `count()` but is not literally that string is left untouched. In practice that includes:

- Aliased forms: `count() as my_count`, `count() AS count`.
- Annotated forms: `count()` followed by other tokens, e.g. `count(), other_col` (already split into separate items so OK), but also `count(error_count)` if it ever appears bare.
- Aggregations wrapped by other functions: `topK(1)(count())`.

The result is that for the same query, some y-axes are upsampled and others are not, mixing weighted and unweighted counts in the same response and producing nonsense totals / charts in the dashboard. The match should be against the leading aggregate token rather than the whole trimmed string.

_are_all_projects_error_upsampled does not validate the allowlist option type

`options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", [])` is used directly with `project_id in allowlist`. If the option is ever misconfigured (set to a string, tuple, generator, etc.), `in` falls back to iteration/substring semantics — for a string allowlist, `123 in "1234"` returns True and arbitrary project IDs will be considered allowlisted, silently enabling upsampling (and inflated counts) for the wrong tenants. There is no schema/option validator in this PR and no isinstance(list)/set coercion in the consumer. Coerce `allowlist` to a `set` (and assert the type) before the membership check.

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling swallows all exceptions with bare except Exception

Both `try: ... except Exception: pass` blocks around the `contexts.error_sampling` lookup and the `float(...)` conversion in `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` silently discard every error. Because this runs on every `store_event` call in tests (and could be wired into production ingestion), any structural change to the event dict (renamed contexts, different nesting, AttributeError on a non-dict `contexts`, etc.) will fail silently and leave `sample_rate` unset with no log/raise. The function should narrow the catch (e.g. `(AttributeError, TypeError, ValueError)`) and at minimum `logger.warning` on unexpected shapes so misconfiguration is debuggable.

The docstring for `_is_error_focused_query` says "Reduced to only check for event.type:error to err on the side of caution", and the surrounding module comment on line 86 likewise claims sample_weight is guaranteed by the schema so no checks are needed. The actual substring check is more permissive than just `event.type:error` (it also matches `!event.type:error`, `event.type:errors`, compound OR queries with transactions), and the sample_weight assumption is not enforced anywhere visible in this PR. These comments will mislead future maintainers into trusting the function's output. Either tighten the implementation to match the comments or update the comments to describe the real behavior.

Denial cache blocks fallback for 30s after permission grants or folder-permission grants

The new permDenialCache is keyed by (namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) with a 30s TTL and is consulted BEFORE the permCache check and the new DB-fallback path. Trace for the regression scenario: (T=0) user denied -> permDenialCache.Set(("dash1", "fold1")) and permCache holds empty data; (T=10) admin grants permission on dash1, or grants permission on fold1 which gives inherited access via checkInheritedPermissions; (T=15) user retries -> permDenialCache.Get HITS and returns Allowed=false, so neither permCache nor getIdentityPermissions is consulted. In OAuthLoginView.dispatch(), `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is called OUTSIDE the try/except block. OAuth authorize URL parameters not URL-encoded

The OAuth authorize URL is built via f-string interpolation: `f"{...}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"`. Neither `state` (currently `pipeline.signature`, an md5 hex digest, so safe today) nor `redirect_uri` is URL-encoded. If `redirect_uri` ever contains reserved characters (`&`, `?`, `=`, `#`, etc.), or if `pipeline.signature` generation changes, GitHub will parse the query string incorrectly and the OAuth callback state verification will fail or — worse — allow query parameters to bleed into `state`/`redirect_uri`. Tracing the flow: the first request to `setup_path` with `installation_id` triggers OAuthLoginView, which redirects to GitHub (no call to the 404 endpoint). The second request carries a hardcoded `state` of `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` that does NOT match the pipeline signature, so OAuthLoginView short-circuits on the state check and returns `error()` before `build_integration` is ever reached. In `test_github_user_mismatch` the webhook is posted with the hardcoded header `HTTP_X_HUB_SIGNATURE="sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486"`, but the request body is `json.dumps(webhook_event)` after the test mutates `installation.id` and `sender.login`. That HMAC was presumably computed over the unmodified `INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE` bytes. Standard GitHub webhook handlers verify the signature against the raw request body and reject mismatches (typically with a 401/403). When the handler rejects the webhook, no `Integration` record with `sender.login == "attacker"` is created, and the subsequent user-mismatch check in `GitHubInstallation` won't fire as intended. Either compute the signature dynamically from the mutated payload using the test webhook secret, or fix the signature for the actual bytes posted. This test should currently be failing or is silently broken.

OAuthLoginView introduces four new error branches that all funnel into the same `error()` helper and are therefore indistinguishable to callers: (1) `state` parameter mismatch, (2) GitHub returning no `access_token` in the token-exchange response, (3) `get_user_info` returning no `login`, and (4) the GitHubInstallation-level user mismatch (which is tested but only via the generic template assertion). Each of these is a distinct failure mode documented in the PR description ("state mismatch", "wrong or re-used code", "authenticate user mismatch") and should have a dedicated test that verifies the request reaches the expected code path and that the failure is rendered. The access token returned will have only the default user:email scope (or whatever GitHub grants by default). `get_user_info` only uses `/user`, which works under the default scope, but if Sentry ever tries to use the resulting token for anything requiring an additional scope (e.g., reading private email, listing org installations), the request will silently 404/403. This is informational; consider either requesting the scopes Sentry actually needs explicitly (`scope=user:email read:org`), or documenting that only the default user-scope token is intended.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsafe SQL formatting pattern retained as dead code

Although the new stub DB returns `"not implemented"` before any statement is actually evaluated, the vulnerable code path is still reachable via `UnmarshalSQLCommand` / `NewSQLCommand`, which are not gated by the new `enableSqlExpressions` check in `reader.go`. Since `TablesList` now always returns the stub error and is never useful, the entire function (and the unsafe `Sprintf`/`Replace`/`RunCommands` calls) should be deleted rather than preserved in a half-disabled form.

Error message claims SQL expressions were never implemented

This message is misleading for two reasons: (a) SQL expressions were shipped and used in dashboards before this PR, so users with existing panels will hit this error and have no way to understand why a previously working feature now fails; (b) the message obscures the actual reason — a security fix for CVE-2024-9264. Future maintainers may reasonably assume this is a working SQL backend and try to fill in the methods to re-enable the feature, reintroducing the vulnerability. Add a comment such as `// Stub DB used after CVE-2024-9264 to make SQL expressions return errors; do not implement.`

Existing tests for `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` (and for `UnmarshalSQLCommand`) will continue to pass only if they don't exercise the `QueryTypeSQL` branch; there is nothing pinning the new behavior. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Thundering herd: no re-check of cache after acquiring write lock

After acquiring the write lock at line 48, the function does not re-check whether entryPointAssetsCache has been populated by another goroutine that passed the fast-path check (lines 41-47) while the cache was still nil. As a result, every concurrent goroutine that observes a nil cache in the fast path will acquire the write lock in turn and each redundantly re-read the manifest file and re-parse the JSON. This is the classic double-checked-locking pitfall: the fast-path RLock/RUnlock check at lines 41-43 is not mirrored inside the Lock-held critical section. At Grafana startup, where many HTTP handlers can call this function concurrently, this causes N redundant file reads and JSON decodes instead of one. The fix is to add a re-check inside the write-lock critical section, e.g. by inserting `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` on line 48.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock, allowing concurrent goroutines that observed an empty cache to redundantly populate it.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test added for the race fix

The PR fixes a data race on the entryPointAssetsCache package variable by adding a sync.RWMutex around its reads and writes. However, no test file is added or modified alongside this change. A regression test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently from multiple goroutines (e.g. via sync.WaitGroup) and runs under `go test -race` would have caught the original race and now guards against future refactors reintroducing it. Without such a test, the fix is unverified by CI and can silently regress.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

...

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The cleanup ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute:
```

+ ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)
```
This is not mentioned in the PR description and is unrelated to the MySQL deadlock fix. It increases the run frequency of *every* job in clean() (tmp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) by 10x, multiplying DB load and the chance of overlapping long-running cleanups against the 9-minute per-cycle timeout. Nil error logged as err field on success

Multiple new log calls include `"err", err` after the error has already been checked and returned (e.g. lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). On the happy path err is nil, so the resulting structured log entry looks like `"err": null` for a successful batch. This is misleading to operators who scan logs for `"err":` fields and makes it look like every cleanup batch is failing. The err key should only be included when an error is actually present.

O(n^2) string building in SQLite large-batch path

The SQLite parameter-limit workaround builds the IN-list with repeated fmt.Sprintf:
```
values := fmt.Sprint(ids[0])
for _, v := range ids[1:] {
    values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)
}
```
This is O(n^2) in both time and allocations because each step copies the entire growing string. With the batch size used in the new test (32767) this is tens of millions of bytes copied. The same job can be done in O(n) with a strings.Builder and strconv.AppendInt. The path is also only triggered when batch size exceeds the SQLite parameter limit, so it is exercised by the new integration test and the cost matters.

fetchIDs concatenates table name and condition into SQL

fetchIDs builds SQL via fmt.Sprintf with the table name and the WHERE clause as opaque strings:
```
sql := fmt.Sprintf(`SELECT id FROM %s`, table)
sql += fmt.Sprintf(` WHERE %s`, condition)
```
Today every call site passes a constant string so there is no immediate injection, but the signature invites future callers to pass user-controlled fragments. Either make the table an enumerated constant or compose the predicate through bound parameters, so the function cannot be misused.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the logging context uses d.Log instead of the enriched log variable, preventing name, kind, and method values from propagating.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records storage metric with name as kind label

In Delete, the success-path metric is `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. All other methods use `options.Kind` as the third argument (the resource-kind label). Passing `name` here will produce a different label cardinality and break any dashboard or alert that aggregates by kind for delete operations. It should be `options.Kind` to be consistent with Create/Update/DeleteCollection and with the legacy-error metric on line 113.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same inconsistency: Delete passes name instead of options.Kind to metrics recording, unlike other methods.

false_positives.candidate:
DeleteCollection records storage metric for legacy call

In the DeleteCollection async goroutine, `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` is called after `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)`. It should be `d.recordLegacyDuration` because the call is to LegacyStorage, not Storage. As written, every legacy delete-collection failure will be misattributed to Storage in metrics, defeating monitoring and SLO alerting on the legacy path.

Create error path records legacy metric using storage timer

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Two problems: (1) it records a legacy duration even though the legacy was never called; (2) the duration it computes is for Storage (startStorage), not Legacy. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. The same bug exists for Update on line 129. Effect: storage failures will be miscounted as legacy failures and the recorded duration will not correspond to the failing call.

Update error path records legacy metric using storage timer

When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Same issue as the Create error path: this should be `d.recordStorageDuration` because the error happened in Storage, and the timer being measured (`startStorage`) corresponds to Storage, not Legacy. Storage update failures will be misattributed to the legacy path in metrics.

Async legacy write derives context from cancelled request context

All four async goroutines (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) build their timeout context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the request context (`klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` from the outer function). When the originating HTTP handler returns, the request context is cancelled and the derived context is immediately cancelled as well, so the 10s timeout is effectively zero. The whole point of mode 3 is to mirror writes to legacy as a safety net; with a cancelled parent context this safety net is dropped on every request that returns before the goroutine schedules. The legacy-mirror call should be made independent of request lifetime (e.g., derive from a long-lived background context) so that the write actually completes after the response is sent.

Same objInfo reused for Storage and Legacy Update calls

`objInfo` is passed to `d.Storage.Update` and then, in the goroutine, to `d.Legacy.Update` unchanged. `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations are commonly stateful (the previous version of this file explicitly wrapped it in `updateWrapper` and supplied a fresh wrapper holding the updated object for the legacy call). Reusing objInfo risks the legacy update either re-fetching the pre-update object, returning stale data, or returning an error from the second `UpdatedObject` invocation. This is a behavioural regression from the prior implementation in this same function.

Async legacy goroutines have no panic recovery

The four `go func()` blocks (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) call into legacy storage and record metrics without any panic recovery. A panic inside the legacy storage adapter or in the metric call will crash the process because Go panics in unrecovered goroutines are fatal. Each goroutine should at minimum `defer recover()` and log the recovered value so that a single failing legacy backend cannot bring down the API server.

defer cancel() placed after side-effecting line in Update goroutine

In the Update goroutine, `defer cancel()` is placed between `startLegacy := time.Now()` and the `d.Legacy.Update` call. While functionally correct (defer runs at function exit), it is stylistically inconsistent with the Create/Delete/DeleteCollection goroutines, which put `defer cancel()` immediately after the `context.WithTimeoutCause` call. Easy fix: move the deferred cancel directly under the WithTimeoutCause call.

Legacy mirror timeout is a hardcoded magic number

`time.Second*10` appears as the timeout for the legacy-mirror context in Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. This should be a configurable constant (or a field on DualWriterMode3) so it can be tuned per resource type and tested; otherwise changing it requires editing four call sites.

TestMode3_Get uses local prometheus registry instead of shared one

Only `TestMode3_Get` creates its own registry with `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()`. Every other TestMode3_* test uses the package-level `p`. The dual-writer change in `dualwriter_mode1_test.go` removed the same leftover in mode1, but the corresponding cleanup was missed in `TestMode3_Get`. Use the shared `p` for consistency and to avoid duplicate registries across tests.

Tests do not verify async legacy write actually occurred

In TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection the legacy call is dispatched in a goroutine after the request returns, but the test only asserts on the synchronous return value. There is no synchronization (no WaitGroup, channel, or `m.AssertExpectations`) to ensure the legacy mock was actually invoked before the test exits. A regression where the goroutine no longer runs (e.g., refactor that accidentally makes the legacy call synchronous-but-skipped) would pass these tests silently. Add a synchronization mechanism (e.g., a `sync.WaitGroup` toggled in the goroutine, or use a channel signaled by a mock callback) and call `m.AssertExpectations(t)` to assert the legacy side effect actually happened.

TestMode3_Create failure case sets up the wrong store's mock

The second test case in TestMode3_Create is named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" and expects `wantErr: true`, but the expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` against the legacy store. Because the test wires both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` to the same `mock.Mock{}`, the expectation ends up firing on whichever call runs first (the storage call), so the test happens to pass for the wrong reason. If the two mocks are ever given separate mock instances, this case will silently flip to passing on the legacy path and the error will be swallowed by the async goroutine. Either rename the case or register the expectation against the storage mock explicitly.

Standard implementations of `applyTemplateVariables` mutate the input query and return it (as evidenced by the test mock at shardQuerySplitting.test.ts lines 56-59). true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit can be exceeded under concurrent load (TOCTOU)

In CreateOrUpdateDevice, the active device count is read with CountDevices and then, based on that single read, either an UPDATE or an INSERT path is taken. There is no row-level lock, advisory lock, or transactional serialization between the count and the subsequent write. Under concurrent requests from different device IDs, two goroutines can both observe count == limit-1, both fall through to the INSERT path, and the resulting row count exceeds the configured AnonymousDeviceLimit. The whole point of this PR is the limit; it must hold under concurrency. Fix by serializing the check+write (e.g. transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a sentinel row, an advisory lock, or pushing the limit enforcement into a single atomic SQL statement).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass the device count check before inserting, causing the device limit to be exceeded. Both recommend transaction or locking-based serialization of the check and write.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Returning devices whose entry is expired are wrongly rejected as 'limit reached'

updateDevice issues `UPDATE anon_device SET ... WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?`, where the BETWEEN range is `device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration)` to `device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(time.Minute)` (i.e. the last 30 days). CountDevices uses the same window, so any device whose updated_at is older than 30 days is NOT counted in the active device count. But the UPDATE WHERE clause filters out that exact row, returning 0 rowsAffected and surfacing ErrDeviceLimitReached. Effect: a returning user whose anon_device row is between 30 and 61 days old (the cleanup interval is 61 days) is denied authentication even though, by the counting rule, there is 'room' for them. The intent of the limit appears to be 'only NEW device_ids are limited; existing device_ids are always updatable'. Match on device_id alone, or look the device up first, before deciding to reject.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: updateDevice maps zero affected rows to ErrDeviceLimitReached even when the update fails because the device falls outside the timestamp window, rather than because a device limit was reached.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous auth now blocks on DB write and request context cancellation

Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine on a fresh context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute) so anonymous authentication never waited on, nor could be aborted by, the DB. The new code calls TagDevice(ctx, ...) synchronously, using the request context. Consequences: (1) every anonymous auth now incurs at least one DB round-trip (CountDevices, plus UPDATE or INSERT) before the identity is returned, (2) if the client disconnects mid-request the request context is cancelled and the tag DB write fails with context.Canceled, (3) any DB slowness or transient error directly delays/fails anonymous logins. The goroutine-and-detached-context design existed precisely to decouple auth from the side-effect DB write. The limit check needed to make auth decisions could be done as a separate read-only query while still keeping the write detached; or the limit check could run in the goroutine and short-circuit a follow-up call.

Panic recovery was removed from the anonymous tag path

The previous goroutine wrapped the TagDevice call in `defer func() { if err := recover(); err != nil { a.log.Warn(...) } }()`. The new synchronous implementation has no panic recovery, so any panic in tagDeviceUI, CreateOrUpdateDevice, or a sqlstore helper will now propagate out of Anonymous.Authenticate and into the request handler. The action body just calls `this.get("model").addMembers(this.get("usernames"))` and ignores the returned promise. On failure the controller does `var message = $.parseJSON(e.responseText).errors;`. That throw is swallowed by the promise chain, `disableSave` is reset to false in `.finally`, and the admin sees no error message at all — the save button just becomes clickable again with no indication that anything went wrong. true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Database write in validator without error handling

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` calls `record.save` without any rescue. It is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, which runs during `User#valid?` / `User#save`. If the save fails (e.g. DB connection blip, lock timeout, race causing a stale `match_count` that triggers a future validation), ActiveRecord raises and the user sees a generic 500 instead of a clean signup error. Validators should be side-effect free and idempotent; the counter increment belongs either in `update_all` (atomic, no exception on no-op) or in an `after_validation` / async job, not inside a validator that runs on every attribute check.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying concern: a blocking check performs a database write to increment statistics, introducing side effects during validation/read operations and potential concurrency problems. Its emphasis on error handling differs, but it explicitly flags the counter update and lack of side-effect-free behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Regex metacharacters in domain setting are not escaped

`email_in_restriction_setting?` only does `setting.gsub('.', '\.')` before building `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)`. The whitelist/blacklist values are admin-controlled site settings that may contain `|`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `+`, `*`, `?`, `^`, `$`, `\`. A value like `gmail.com|mail.ru` would match `@gmail.com` *or* `@mail.ru` (the first `|` makes `mail.ru` a separate alternative of the whole group, not a literal). Also, because the pattern is `@(...)` with no anchors, a blacklist value of `mail.ru` already matches `user@mail.ru.example.com`. Escape all regex metacharacters and anchor the match (e.g. require the domain to end at a non-word character or end of string) so neither false positives nor ReDoS-via-admin-setting is possible.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate primarily discusses unescaped metacharacters, it also explicitly identifies the same unanchored domain-matching regex and recommends domain boundary anchoring. This matches the golden comment's underlying concern about matching partial domains rather than complete domains.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case- and whitespace-sensitive

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs a literal equality match, and `BlockedEmail` neither downcases nor strips the email on save. The rest of the codebase treats email as case-insensitive (`User.find_by_username_or_email` downcases via `Email.downcase`, `users_controller#change_email` strips and downcases). A user can trivially bypass a block by signing up with `BAD@spamclub.com`, `bad@spamclub.com ` (trailing space), etc., and the same bypass defeats the admin's intent when they later look up rows in `blocked_emails`. Normalize the email (downcase + strip) on both write (`before_validation`) and read inside `should_block?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? that allows differently capitalized emails to bypass a block. Its additional whitespace concern does not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
Lost-update race in match_count increment

`record.match_count += 1; record.save` is a read-modify-write on a single row with no row lock. Under any concurrent signups for the same blocked address (and Discourse runs Puma/clustered workers), two callers can both read e.g. `match_count = 5`, both bump to 6, and both persist 6 — losing one increment. The same problem affects `last_match_at`. Use an atomic SQL update, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(["match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", Time.zone.now])`, so the counter cannot be lost.

The spec only covers the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch via Mocha stubs. The whitelist and blacklist branches (the original purpose of `email_validator`, moved out of `User`) are completely untested. Without covering those, a regression that, say, swaps the `if`/`elsif` to make blacklist override whitelist, or one that breaks the regex escape, would pass tests. Add at least one case each for: (a) whitelist present, email not in whitelist -> error added, (b) whitelist present, email in whitelist -> no error, (c) blacklist present, email in blacklist -> error added, (d) blacklist present, email not in blacklist -> no error, and (e) error from whitelist suppresses the BlockedEmail branch.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

include_website_name predicate missing '?' suffix

The new predicate `def include_website_name` is defined without the trailing question mark, breaking the ActiveModel::Serializer convention used by every other include_* method in this file (include_email?, include_stats?, include_suspend_reason?, include_card_image_badge?, etc.). ActiveModel::Serializer looks specifically for `include_<attr>?` to gate attribute serialization. As a result the predicate is never invoked and `website_name` is always included in the serialized JSON whenever the attribute is defined, regardless of the intended `website.present?` check. This also defeats any future attempt to gate website_name exposure (e.g. for TL0 users via untrusted_attributes, since the predicate won't fire).

The new `website_name` implementation has three branches (exact match, `www.example.com == forum.example.com` style same-suffix with equal part count > 2, and parent-domain suffix). The spec only exercises the first and third (`Discourse.stubs(:current_hostname).returns('example.com')` and `...('forums.example.com')`); the elsif branch with two 3-part hosts sharing a suffix (e.g. `www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com`, both returning the full path) has no test, so a regression there would not be caught.

URI(website.to_s) parsed three times per call

`website_name` calls `URI(website.to_s)` three times to extract `.host` and `.path`. Since `website` is a method that reads `object.user_profile.website`, the value is stable across calls within one invocation, but parsing the URL three times is wasteful and makes the logic fragile: any future change that makes `website` non-deterministic (e.g., conditional computation) would cause `.host` and `.path` to be taken from different URLs. Hoisting `uri = URI(website.to_s)` (inside the existing `rescue`) into a local would fix both concerns.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses indexOf substring match

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` checks whether `e.origin` appears anywhere inside `discourseUrl` rather than comparing the origin exactly. Even though discourseUrl is configured by the embedding site, a confused deployer can be tricked into rejecting legitimate messages or accepting unexpected ones if the configured URL embeds other origins as substrings. true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer-based authorization is fragile and bypassable

`ensure_embeddable` only checks `URI(request.referer || '').host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The Referer header is freely spoofable in many environments (browsers with privacy extensions, server-side fetchers, embedded webviews, curl), it can be wholly absent (in which case the empty string still passes URI parsing and compares mismatched, denying the request), and the comparison is a plain string match that ignores ports/scheme. An attacker able to set Referer (or to load the embed URL from a non-browser context) can pretend to come from any host. Authorization must not rely on a header that the configured embeddable host cannot enforce, and should additionally match scheme/port (e.g. compare `host_with_port` and `scheme`). At minimum, the current check must be paired with a signed/shared-secret or signed embed_url before the controller will fetch arbitrary content from the Discourse server.

Although it omits the ALLOWALL header and frames the impact as authorization rather than clickjacking, it captures the underlying security concern of relying on a spoofable Referer check.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. On top of that, the surrounding code never validates the feed URL protocol, content type, or item count, and never catches network or parse errors, so a single malformed item or transient feed failure kills the whole job. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: RSS items may have nil content, causing i.content.scrub to raise NoMethodError. Although it suggests a nil guard rather than a description fallback and includes additional concerns, the core issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

Inside `<script>`, HTML entities such as `'` are unescaped by the JS parser back to `'` before execution, so a parent page can supply a referer like `https://x'); alert(1); //` and execute attacker JS in the embed iframe. Migration backfills cook_method=1 (raw_html) for every post, breaking cooking pipeline

`add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false` sets the integer 1 as the default for all existing rows and for every future insert that omits cook_method. But `Post.cook_methods` is defined as `Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)` in app/models/post.rb, where the Enum assigns sequential indices starting at 0, so `:regular == 0` and `:raw_html == 1`. The migration therefore marks every existing post as raw_html. After deployment, `before_save` (`self.cooked = cook(raw, topic_id: topic_id) unless new_record?`) calls `Post#cook`, which now short-circuits to `return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, so the first edit on any previously-rendered post overwrites `cooked` with raw markdown and breaks rendering for that post and every post that quotes/redisplays it.

Post.cook short-circuits to raw_html because the migration default points at the raw_html enum value

`return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` is gated on the raw_html enum value, but the DB default set by the new migration (default: 1) and every PostCreator call that does not explicitly pass `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:regular]` will land on raw_html. Combined with the migration defaulting all rows to 1, every legacy post and every default-created post loses its cooked HTML. The intent appears to be that `raw_html` is opt-in (only the embed/RSS import path sets it), so the enum value used for the column default must be `:regular` (0) and any feed/import caller should pass the raw_html value explicitly. Right now, both kinds of writes converge on raw_html, corrupting posts.

TopicRetriever invokes scheduled feed poll synchronously inside an embed job

`Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` is called inline inside `perform_retrieve` whenever `SiteSetting.feed_polling_enabled?` is true. PollFeed is a recurring scheduled job that fetches the full configured RSS/ATOM feed and imports every item; running it synchronously inside an embed fetch blocks the worker for the full poll duration, doubles the load on the feed endpoint (once from the scheduled worker, once from each embed call), and re-imports items outside the dedup logic embedded in TopicEmbed.import. It should enqueue the scheduled job via Sidekiq or at minimum only check `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: ...)` without triggering a full re-poll.

NoMethodError when SiteSetting.embed_by_username is blank

`User.where(username_lower: SiteSetting.embed_by_username.downcase).first` calls `.downcase` on the setting value without first verifying it is non-nil. PollFeed guards against this with the `SiteSetting.embed_by_username.present?` check, but `TopicRetriever#fetch_http` does not, so a missing setting raises NoMethodError, which propagates out of the retrieve_topic job. force: true silently drops and recreates the top_topics table

Changing `create_table :top_topics` to `create_table :top_topics, force: true` makes the migration drop any pre-existing `top_topics` table before recreating it. The migration was previously already shipped to production; if any environment has a partially applied state, the next migration run will silently destroy data. Either drop the existing migration in favor of a new one that no-ops for upgrades, or document that this change must run on a clean DB only.

Unused require_dependency 'email/sender'

The job requires `email/sender` but never references it (and TopicRetriever does not either). Remove the unused dependency to avoid loading unnecessary code paths and to prevent surprising coupling when email/Sender changes.

Tests do not cover the perform_retrieve (SSRF and dedup) paths

The spec only exercises the gated path through `retrieve` and asserts that `perform_retrieve` is or isn't called. There is no coverage of `perform_retrieve`, `fetch_http`, the `Jobs::PollFeed` invocation, or the duplicate-embed short-circuit. SSRF (fetching arbitrary URLs via `import_remote`) and the dedup queries are security-/data-integrity-sensitive and should have explicit specs covering the host check inside perform_retrieve, the user lookup, and the `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url:).exists?` early-return.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

Client upload size cap hardcoded to 10MB, bypassing the site setting

`validateUploadedFile` previously read the cap from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, supporting independent `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb`. It is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024` for every type. Consequences: (1) administrators lose the ability to tighten or loosen the client-side cap; (2) when an admin sets `max_image_size_kb` lower than 10MB the client still accepts up to 10MB and the user only finds out the upload is too large after the round trip; (3) the previous per-type distinction between images and attachments is lost. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same hardcoded 10MB limit overriding per-type site settings and causing client/server limit divergence. Not mentioning the 413 handler does not change the underlying issue match.

5 downsize iterations are mathematically insufficient for the feature to work

Each pass uses `"80%"` dimensions, which shrinks image area to 0.8² = 0.64 of the original, so the file size drops by roughly 36% per iteration. After 5 iterations the file is approximately 0.64⁵ ≈ 33% of the original. With the default `max_image_size_kb` of 10MB, any source image above ~30MB cannot be brought under the limit in 5 passes; for example a 50MB image ends up at ~16MB and a 100MB image at ~33MB. The `while` loop then exits and `Upload.create_for` is invoked with an oversized file, so the 'auto-downsize' feature silently fails for any but moderately large images. Either the iteration count must scale with the initial size, the reduction factor must be more aggressive, or the loop should compute the required scale per iteration and pass it to `OptimizedImage.downsize`.

413 error message shows hardcoded 10MB instead of configured limit

The 413 branch of `displayErrorForUpload` previously displayed `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` in the user-facing `file_too_large` error. It now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024`, so the size quoted in the error dialog no longer matches the actual configured `max_image_size_kb`. Users will see '10MB' even when the real limit is 2MB or 50MB, leading to confusing UX after any admin change to the site setting.

In-place downsize overwrites source file and ignores failure

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` reads from and writes to the same path. If the convert/gifsicle invocation fails (corrupt input, OOM, signal, bad permissions), ImageMagick may truncate or zero out the file before erroring, and the loop never checks the return value (`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns true/false), so the next iteration or the subsequent `Upload.create_for` will run on a corrupted/empty file. The fix is to write to a separate temp path, verify the result, then atomically rename, and to break out of the loop when downsize reports failure rather than blindly iterating again.

`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces the previous cap of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. When an admin raises `max_image_size_kb` above 10MB (e.g. 50MB), the URL fetch path will now reject with a download error for any source between 10MB and the configured limit, even though the upload is supposed to be allowed and auto-downsized. Conversely, when the admin lowers `max_image_size_kb` to e.g. 1MB, the download limit is 10x the upload limit, which is intentional for downsizing but is not surfaced as a setting. The download cap should be a separate, larger setting (or derived as `max_image_size_kb * N`) rather than a hardcoded 10MB.

OptimizedImage.optimize arity changed from 6 to 5

`def self.optimize(operation, from, to, width, height, opts={})` (5 positional args + opts) is replaced by `def self.optimize(operation, from, to, dimensions, opts={})` (4 positional args + opts). Although this method is more internal than `downsize`, it is still a public class method, and any external caller (e.g. plugins or specs) passing separate width/height integers will now get those values joined as `"800600"` and passed to ImageMagick, which is silently wrong. The arity change should be paired with explicit deprecation or a new method name to avoid silent breakage.

false_positives.candidate:
List-Unsubscribe header still points at global preferences, not the per-topic URL

In `header_args`, the RFC8058 one-click `List-Unsubscribe` header is set to `template_args[:user_preferences_url]` even though `@opts[:unsubscribe_url]` (the new per-topic URL, which is the entire point of this PR) is now available and merged into `template_args`. Mail clients such as Gmail, Apple Mail and Outlook honor this header to render a one-click "Unsubscribe" button; users who click it will be sent to the global preferences page and effectively unsubscribed from all email, not just this topic. The header should use `template_args[:unsubscribe_url]` when present, so the standard one-click path matches the in-body link.

GET endpoint mutates a user's notification level with no CSRF protection or signed token `TopicsController#unsubscribe` is wired as a GET route (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe" => "topics#unsubscribe"`) and silently calls `tu.save!` to change the logged-in user's notification level. The `ensure_logged_in` filter only requires a session; it provides no CSRF defense, and there is no signed token in the URL analogous to the existing `email/unsubscribe/:key` mechanism. Any third-party site can embed `` and, when a logged-in Discourse user loads the page, their topic notification state is changed without consent. State-changing actions triggered from email should either use a signed, single-use key (as the global email unsubscribe already does) or be a POST guarded by a CSRF token / explicit confirmation step.

Toggle logic only mutes users already at regular; watching/tracking users keep getting emails

The branch `if tu.notification_level > TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular]` sets the level to `:regular` for users at `:tracking` or `:watching`, and only sets `:muted` for users already at `:regular` or `:muted`. With the notification levels enum (muted=0, regular=1, tracking=2, watching=3), a user who was watching the topic and clicks unsubscribe is downgraded to `regular`, which still produces email notifications for every reply. The user-visible text in `topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications` says "You will stop receiving notifications", which is false for that common case. The action should either jump straight to `:muted` (matching the wording) or clearly document that the first click is a "reduce" and the second is a "mute".

Test for List-Unsubscribe header only checks presence, not that the per-topic URL is used

The existing test `it "has an List-Unsubscribe header"` only asserts that the header is `be_present`, even though the new test setup now passes `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"`. Because the assertion doesn't compare the header value, it would still pass if the header were (incorrectly) hard-coded to the global preferences URL. The test should assert that `header_args['List-Unsubscribe']` includes the per-topic `unsubscribe_url`, so the regression in `message_builder.rb#header_args` is caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BSD sed syntax breaks on Linux

The line `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses the BSD/macOS form `sed -i ''` where the empty argument is the backup-extension placeholder. On GNU sed (the default on the Linux/CI environments this repo targets), `-i ''` is parsed as `-i` followed by `''` and then `-E`, causing errors like `sed: can't read E: No such file or directory`, so the .env update silently fails and the rest of the script can't restore GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL. Detect the platform (e.g. `[[ $OSTYPE == darwin* ]] && sed_i() { sed -i '' "$@"; } || sed_i() { sed -i "$@"; }`) or use a portable alternative such as `sed -i.bak ... && rm "$ENV_FILE.bak"`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same portability bug: the BSD/macOS `sed -i ''` syntax fails on GNU sed on Linux.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

Throwing a bare Error here skips tRPC's code propagation: the client receives an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR with a 500 status for what is really a 404 / 403, and the toast in CredentialActionsDropdown cannot distinguish 'not found' from 'permission denied' from a transient DB error. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: throwing a plain Error for an authentication or access-denied failure causes tRPC to return a 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR instead of a structured TRPCError with an appropriate status. The suggested error codes differ, but the underlying bug is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status ignores expiry, marking stale rows as fresh

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds uses prisma.calendarCache.groupBy to find the most recent updatedAt for each credential, but it does not constrain expiresAt to be in the future. The UI displays a 'Cache Status' timestamp whenever a row exists, even when all matching rows are expired (cache TTL is 30 days, set in upsertCachedAvailability via CACHING_TIME). Because getCachedAvailability itself filters by expiresAt >= now, the user is shown what looks like valid cache data for credentials whose cache is actually invalid. Add `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }` to the where clause so the UI only surfaces still-valid cache.

deleteCache success does not invalidate connectedCalendars

After deleting the cache the mutation only shows a toast and calls onSuccess?.(); it never invalidates the viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars query. The sibling disconnectMutation on lines 53-65 explicitly invalidates utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars and utils.viewer.apps.integrations on settle, which keeps the dropdown and parent list in sync. The deletion path lacks the same invalidation, so after a successful Delete cached data the dropdown continues to render the 'Cache Status' row with the previous timestamp and the 'Delete cached data' item, and the parent's ConnectedCalendarList still shows the now-stale cacheUpdatedAt. Add an invalidate of utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars (and ideally utils.viewer.apps.integrations) in onSuccess or onSettled.

updateManyByCredentialId invoked with empty data

`await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` passes an empty data object, which only does anything because Prisma auto-bumps `@updatedAt`. Without that hidden schema behavior this would be a no-op (or even a validation error in some Prisma versions), so the intent ('bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under this credential') is implicit and brittle. Pass the timestamp explicitly, e.g. `data: { updatedAt: new Date() }`, and document that the field exists at the call site.

Migration comment does not match SQL

The header comment warns: 'Added the required column `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty.' DropdownMenuItem used for non-interactive cache info

Use a non-interactive primitive such as a `<div>` or `<DropdownMenuLabel>` for the read-only cache status row and reserve DropdownMenuItem for the Delete cached data choice below.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours end uses slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

In the new working-hours check in `checkIfIsAvailable`, `end` is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` — the same value as `start`. It should be `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()`. Consequence: the `end > workingHour.endTime` half of the condition can never trigger, so a slot that starts inside working hours but whose end spills past `workingHour.endTime` (e.g. working hours 09:00–17:00, slot 16:30–17:30) is incorrectly treated as inside working hours. With a 60-minute event this can return bookable slots that extend past the organizer's day.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the exact same bug: the end time is calculated using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === instead of isSame

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly-constructed Dayjs objects with strict equality. Dayjs objects are compared by reference, so this branch is unreachable. The intent appears to be "override has zero duration / is empty", which should be `…isSame(…)`. Consequence: an empty/zero-length date override is never short-circuited and the surrounding code falls through to the other boundary checks, which can produce wrong availability when start and end coincide.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: strict equality compares distinct Dayjs object references rather than their date values, making the condition false. Both recommend using .isSame() instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours day/hour/minute read from UTC, not organizer tz

`slotStartTime` is `time.utc()`, so `slotStartTime.day()`, `.hour()` and `.minute()` return UTC values, while `workingHours` are stored in the organizer's timezone. The membership check `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` and the minute comparison will be wrong near day boundaries or for organizers not in UTC (e.g. a slot at 23:30 IST = 18:00 UTC will be checked against the UTC day/hour instead of the IST day/hour). This can return slots outside the organizer's working day or filter out slots that should be available.

Date-override day match is compared in UTC, not organizer tz

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` compares two UTC-formatted dates. The date override is a calendar day in the organizer's timezone, and `slotStartTime` is in UTC. Around the day boundary (e.g. override on 2024-01-01 IST = 2023-12-31 18:30 UTC …) a slot on the correct local day can be compared against the wrong UTC date and the override will be silently ignored. Use the organizer's timezone for both sides of the comparison (e.g. `dayjs.tz(slotStartTime, organizerTimeZone).format(...)`).

Override boundary check is strict, missing same-instant starts

`slotStartTime.isAfter(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` is strict: a slot whose start equals the override end is not filtered, and slots that straddle the override end (e.g. override 14:00–18:00, slot 17:30–18:30) are also not filtered because there is no check that the slot end is within the override. The check should also require `slotStartTime` not to be after `date.end` (use `isSameOrAfter` or also verify the slot end) and the same boundary issue applies to `date.start` (a slot that begins before the override starts but ends inside it slips through).

checkIfIsAvailable ignores override.timeZone, uses caller-supplied organizerTimeZone

`dateOverrides` are flattened with `timeZone: availability.timeZone` attached, but `checkIfIsAvailable`'s signature drops that field (type is `{ start: Date; end: Date }[]`) and instead uses the caller-supplied `organizerTimeZone` to compute the UTC offset for `date.start`. If a date override was created in a timezone different from the one currently passed as `organizerTimeZone` (e.g. round-robin where a fixed host's override was stored with one tz and `schedule.timeZone` resolves to another, or DST boundary), the override's intended local time will be misinterpreted, returning the wrong availability.

override.start.toString() parsed in server local tz, then re-zoned

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` first stringifies a Date (which embeds the server's local timezone offset) and parses it back, then re-zones. The resulting `utcOffset` depends on the server's TZ rather than being a pure UTC interpretation. On any server not running in UTC the organizer/invitee offset values (and therefore the computed `offset` and the resulting `startTime`/`endTime`) will be wrong. Use `dayjs.utc(override.start)` (or pass the Date directly) before `.tz(...)`.

override startTime/endTime computed in UTC, not invitee local time

`dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + …` produces the hour/minute of the shifted UTC instant, but the surrounding `buildSlots` compares these values to `dayStart` which is in the invitee's local timezone. The result is that for two invitees in different timezones the same `startTime` value yields the same UTC slot, regardless of invitee tz. This is exactly the behavior the PR description claims to fix ("date overrides didn't adjust to different timezones"). The correct computation is the override's start in the invitee's local tz, e.g. `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).hour() * 60 + dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).minute()`.

New test asserts same UTC slots for two different invitee timezones

The new `scheduleForEventOnADayWithDateOverrideDifferentTimezone` case calls `getSchedule` with `timeZone: "Asia/Dhaka"` and expects the identical UTC slots `[08:30, 09:30, 10:30, 11:30]` as the IST case, with the comment "it should return the same as this is the utc time". The PR description says the fix makes date overrides adjust to the attendee's timezone, so two invitees in materially different timezones (e.g. IST vs America/Los_Angeles) should see different UTC slots. The test as written locks in the pre-fix behavior and will not catch a regression of the stated bug; it also only spans a 30-minute tz difference which doesn't expose the problem at all.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No guard against concurrent cron execution; duplicate SMS and lost retryCount increments possible

The handler reads `unscheduledReminders`, calls the external `twilio.scheduleSMS`, and then updates `workflowReminder` in separate non-transactional steps. There is no lock, advisory mutex, or single-runner coordination. If two cron instances overlap (e.g., the previous run is still in flight when a new one starts, or this cron is invoked manually while a scheduled run is active), both will fetch the same unscheduled rows, both will call `twilio.scheduleSMS` (producing duplicate SMS messages for end users), and both will perform `update` based on the same `retryCount` snapshot so one increment is effectively a no-op. The newly added retry logic amplifies this: if retryCount increments are lost due to the race, a reminder may need more than 2 actual failures before being cleaned up, or conversely may be deleted after only one observed failure. At minimum, the handler should use an advisory lock keyed on the workflow step or use an idempotent update (`update where retryCount = <stale value>`) to make the increment safe.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies updates based on the same stale retryCount snapshot causing lost increments under concurrency, which is the golden comment's underlying issue. Its additional duplicate-SMS concern and different proposed mitigation do not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteMany retryCount branch lacks method filter, can delete non-SMS reminders

The new OR clause in the cleanup deleteMany only filters by `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` on the second branch, with no `method` constraint. The first branch correctly restricts to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`, but the retryCount branch will match WorkflowReminder rows of any method (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) if their retryCount ever exceeds 1. While this PR only increments retryCount for SMS, this is a latent bug: any future code path (or out-of-band DB change) that pushes an EMAIL/WHATSAPP reminder's retryCount above 1 will cause it to be silently deleted by this SMS handler. The retry branch should be `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` to keep the cleanup semantically consistent with the rest of the handler, which only processes SMS.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing WorkflowMethods.SMS filter in the retryCount > 1 branch of the deletion OR clause, which can incorrectly delete non-SMS reminders such as Email and WhatsApp.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests cover the new retry-count / cleanup behavior

The change introduces new persistence logic (a new column, conditional increment in two branches, and a new cleanup predicate) but no test files were added or updated. There is no coverage verifying: (a) `retryCount` is incremented when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy, (b) `retryCount` is incremented in the catch branch, (c) reminders with `retryCount > 1` are deleted regardless of scheduledDate, (d) past-dated SMS reminders without retries are still deleted, or (e) the off-by-one threshold (2 failures -> delete) matches the PR description. Without tests, regressions in the retry threshold or in the OR-clause semantics (e.g., the missing method filter noted above) can ship undetected.

Error log does not identify which reminder failed

The catch block logs only `Error scheduling SMS with error ${error}`. It does not include the reminder id, booking uid, workflowStepId, scheduledDate, sendTo, or the prior retryCount value. When the new retry-and-delete flow drops a reminder (after retryCount > 1) there is no operator-visible trail of which reminder was deleted or why it was abandoned, which makes production debugging and audit of dropped SMS reminders very difficult. At minimum the log line should include the reminder id and the new retryCount.

Cleanup deletes reminders based on retryCount even when scheduledDate is still in the future

The new OR clause causes any WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 to be deleted regardless of its scheduledDate. So if SMS scheduling fails twice for a reminder that is still scheduled to fire hours or days in the future, the reminder is permanently dropped even though the event has not happened yet. This matches the PR description but is worth flagging: there is no alerting or metric when a future reminder is given up on, and no way to distinguish "transient Twilio failure" from "permanent bad phone number". Consider also classifying errors so permanent failures (e.g., invalid phone number from Twilio) are dropped immediately while transient ones use more retries, or at least log when a future-dated reminder is being dropped.

true_positives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

The bug pre-existed in the WhereInput form but is reproduced verbatim in the new SQL, and the new tests do not cover the no-sub-teams case.

false_positives.candidate:
findMany method removed without updating callers

The `findMany` method that previously executed the authorization/filter query through `prisma.bookingTimeStatusDenormalized.findMany` has been removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions()` plus a `prisma.$queryRaw` interpolation. The integration test was migrated to the new shape, but no other callers are updated in this PR. If any HTTP route, tRPC procedure, scheduled job, or other service in the repository invokes `InsightsBookingService.findMany(...)`, those call sites will now fail to compile and/or at runtime. Either the call sites must be migrated in this PR or a transitional shim should be added so the change is non-breaking.

Org-scope test depends on undefined query/Set ordering

The org-scope assertion compares against literal array orderings `[testData.org.id, testData.team.id, team2.id, team3.id]` and `[testData.user.id, user2.id, user3.id]`. These come from `TeamRepository.findAllByParentId`, `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, and `Array.from(new Set(userIdsFromOrg))`. None of those queries specify `ORDER BY`, so the order is implementation-defined and can vary across PostgreSQL versions, under concurrent load, or with different planner settings. A `toEqual` on `Prisma.sql` template literals compares the embedded `.values` arrays by deep equality, so any reorder will fail the test. Either add deterministic ordering on the repository queries, or normalize both sides of the assertion (e.g. compare by `Set` membership, or use a helper that re-sorts the array values) so the test is not order-sensitive.

Invalid-options test bypasses TypeScript via `null as any`

The constructor parameter is declared `options: InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` (required, non-null), but the test for "invalid options" passes `options: null as any` and relies on `safeParse` returning `{ success: false }` so `this.options` ends up `null` and `NOTHING_CONDITION` is produced. This hides a real design question: invalid options silently turn the caller into an unauthorized principal instead of throwing, which means a production bug that constructs an `InsightsBookingService` with a malformed `options` object would just return no data rather than fail loudly. The constructor should either throw on invalid input, or its type should be widened to `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions | null | undefined` so callers can express intent without resorting to `as any`. The current arrangement also means the runtime contract is weaker than the type signature suggests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"

If the parsed response has no `refresh_token` field, the function sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Storing the literal string "refresh_token" and later sending it to Google's/MS's refresh endpoint will cause the next refresh to fail with `invalid_grant`, which the Google service interprets as "unrecoverable, mark credential invalid". Instead, the existing refresh token should be preserved when the response omits one.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: a missing refresh_token in the OAuth refresh response is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token", causing subsequent refresh attempts and authentication to fail.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Minimum token schema is malformed and does not validate anything

The schema is declared as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. `z.string().toString()` evaluates to the literal string `"z.string()"` and Zod's `z.object` does not support arbitrary computed keys this way — it emits a warning at schema construction and the dynamic entries do not actually constrain any property. The resulting schema is effectively `{ access_token: string }` with an additional unknown catch-all, so `refresh_token`, `expiry_date`, `expires_in`, scopes, etc. are not enforced. The function should instead take the provider-specific `schema` argument when credential sharing is enabled (since the shared endpoint returns whatever format the host chose) or declare the real required fields.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same malformed minimumTokenResponseSchema and specifically flags the computed keys using z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString(). Although it describes different runtime consequences, it targets the same underlying schema bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Saves SafeParseReturnType envelope instead of parsed data into credential.key

After the change, the code does `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema); await prisma.credential.update({ ..., data: { key } })`. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the full Zod `SafeParseReturnType` (an object with `success`, `data`, and possibly `error`), not the parsed key.
