The new routes `put "members" => "groups#add_members"` and `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"` are declared at the top level of `resources :groups, constraints: AdminConstraint.new do ... end` (i.e., not inside a `collection do` block), so Rails generates them as MEMBER routes `PUT/DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members`. The corresponding JS (`Discourse.ajax('/admin/groups/' + this.get('id') + '/members.json', ...)`) matches those URLs, so the param that holds the group id is `params[:id]`. However, both new actions read the group with `Group.find(params.require(:group_id).to_i)` (line 66 for add_members, line 85 for remove_member). Because `params[:group_id]` is never populated by the router, every real PUT/DELETE from the admin UI will raise `ActionController::ParameterMissing` and the add/remove member functionality will be completely broken in production. The controller specs pass because RSpec controller specs bypass routing and inject `group_id:` directly into the params hash, which is exactly the test gap that hides this bug. Either change the actions to read `params[:id]`/`params.require(:id)`, or add a `:group_id` segment to the routes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the route supplies the group id as params[:id], but the code reads params[:group_id], so the group membership actions fail.

false_positives.candidate:
addMembers never clears usernames and never reports errors

The action body just calls `this.get("model").addMembers(this.get("usernames"))` and ignores the returned promise. The `// TODO: should clear the input` comment acknowledges the problem: after a successful add, the user-selector still contains the same text, so a second click re-submits the same usernames (silently de-duplicated server-side but still wasteful and confusing). Because no `.then`/`.catch` is wired up either, any failure from the underlying PUT (e.g. the parameter bug described above, or a validation error) is swallowed: the spinner clears, the input keeps the value, and the admin gets no feedback at all. The input should be cleared on success and any error should be surfaced.

add_members splits usernames on comma without trimming or rejecting blanks

`usernames.split(",").each do |username| ... User.find_by_username(username)` is called verbatim on each substring. If the user-selector ever produces a name with surrounding whitespace (e.g. `"alice , bob"` or stray trailing whitespace from an autocomplete suggestion), `User.find_by_username(" alice ")` returns nil and the entry is silently dropped — the request still returns `success_json`, the admin sees "added" and no user was actually added. The code should also explicitly skip blank entries instead of relying on `find_by_username("")` returning nil. Similar trimming is performed in other parts of the app (e.g. user creation) and would be expected here.

Stray closing inside {{#each}} block produces malformed HTML Inside `{{#each m in members}}` there is a literal `` on line 19 with no matching opening `
`, all of which sits inside a ``/`` structure. This is leftover from a previous container-based layout that survived the model refactor. Browsers will auto-correct the DOM in inconsistent ways and it is invalid markup, so any tooling that relies on the parse tree (a11y, sanitizers, etc.) can be confused. The `` should be removed.

save error handler crashes on non-JSON error responses

On failure the controller does `var message = $.parseJSON(e.responseText).errors;`. If the server returns a non-JSON body (e.g. an HTML 500 page from an unhandled exception, a maintenance page, or an empty body for a network failure), `$.parseJSON` throws a `SyntaxError`. That throw is swallowed by the promise chain, `disableSave` is reset to false in `.finally`, and the admin sees no error message at all — the save button just becomes clickable again with no indication that anything went wrong. The handler should guard against parse failure (try/catch or typeof check) and fall back to a generic error or `e.responseText` itself.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Database write in validator without error handling

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` calls `record.save` without any rescue. It is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, which runs during `User#valid?` / `User#save`. If the save fails (e.g. DB connection blip, lock timeout, race causing a stale `match_count` that triggers a future validation), ActiveRecord raises and the user sees a generic 500 instead of a clean signup error. Validators should be side-effect free and idempotent; the counter increment belongs either in `update_all` (atomic, no exception on no-op) or in an `after_validation` / async job, not inside a validator that runs on every attribute check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point at the same problem: the check method (should_block?) writes stats and saves the record during what should be a read/validation. The candidate says validators should be side-effect free, notes the race risk with match_count, and suggests an atomic update. Its framing leans on error handling, but the core concern overlaps.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Regex metacharacters in domain setting are not escaped

`email_in_restriction_setting?` only does `setting.gsub('.', '\.')` before building `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)`. The whitelist/blacklist values are admin-controlled site settings that may contain `|`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `+`, `*`, `?`, `^`, `$`, `\`. A value like `gmail.com|mail.ru` would match `@gmail.com` *or* `@mail.ru` (the first `|` makes `mail.ru` a separate alternative of the whole group, not a literal). Also, because the pattern is `@(...)` with no anchors, a blacklist value of `mail.ru` already matches `user@mail.ru.example.com`. Escape all regex metacharacters and anchor the match (e.g. require the domain to end at a non-word character or end of string) so neither false positives nor ReDoS-via-admin-setting is possible.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment is about missing anchoring: the pattern can match a domain that has extra text attached to the listed one, so whitelist matching is unsafe. The candidate's main point is unescaped regex metacharacters, which is a separate concern. It also explicitly says the `@(...)` pattern has no anchors and gives a partial-match example (mail.ru matching mail.ru.example.com). It recommends anchoring the match. Its example uses the blacklist and a trailing-extension case rather than the golden's subdomain bypass of the whitelist, but the underlying lack-of-anchoring flaw is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case- and whitespace-sensitive

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs a literal equality match, and `BlockedEmail` neither downcases nor strips the email on save. The rest of the codebase treats email as case-insensitive (`User.find_by_username_or_email` downcases via `Email.downcase`, `users_controller#change_email` strips and downcases). A user can trivially bypass a block by signing up with `BAD@spamclub.com`, `bad@spamclub.com ` (trailing space), etc., and the same bypass defeats the admin's intent when they later look up rows in `blocked_emails`. Normalize the email (downcase + strip) on both write (`before_validation`) and read inside `should_block?`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same flaw: should_block? does a case-sensitive email lookup, so a block can be bypassed with a differently-cased email. The candidate also mentions whitespace, which goes beyond the golden comment, but the core issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Lost-update race in match_count increment

`record.match_count += 1; record.save` is a read-modify-write on a single row with no row lock. Under any concurrent signups for the same blocked address (and Discourse runs Puma/clustered workers), two callers can both read e.g. `match_count = 5`, both bump to 6, and both persist 6 — losing one increment. The same problem affects `last_match_at`. Use an atomic SQL update, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(["match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", Time.zone.now])`, so the counter cannot be lost.

EmailValidator spec does not exercise whitelist/blacklist paths

The spec only covers the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch via Mocha stubs. The whitelist and blacklist branches (the original purpose of `email_validator`, moved out of `User`) are completely untested. Without covering those, a regression that, say, swaps the `if`/`elsif` to make blacklist override whitelist, or one that breaks the regex escape, would pass tests. Add at least one case each for: (a) whitelist present, email not in whitelist -> error added, (b) whitelist present, email in whitelist -> no error, (c) blacklist present, email in blacklist -> error added, (d) blacklist present, email not in blacklist -> no error, and (e) error from whitelist suppresses the BlockedEmail branch.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid CSS property `-ms-align-items` emitted by align-items mixin

The mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`, which is not a valid CSS property. The IE10 vendor prefix for align-items is `-ms-flex-align` (already included on the preceding line). Sass will compile this and ship it to the browser, where it is parsed as an unknown declaration and ignored. It also fails strict CSS validation and can produce warnings in tooling. The line should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say -ms-align-items is not a valid property and that the correct IE prefix is -ms-flex-align. They describe the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
`order: 2` applied to a non-flex child has no effect

`@include order(2)` is added to `.extra-info-wrapper`, but its parent `.title-wrapper` is styled in this same file as `float: left; width: 90%;` and is not a flex container. The `order` property only affects flex/grid items, so this declaration is dead CSS in the rendered output. If the intent was to reorder `.extra-info-wrapper` relative to the title, the author likely also needs `@include flexbox()` on `.title-wrapper` (and an explicit order for the other children). Otherwise the line should be removed because it implies a layout change that will not happen.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name predicate missing '?' suffix

The new predicate `def include_website_name` is defined without the trailing question mark, breaking the ActiveModel::Serializer convention used by every other include_* method in this file (include_email?, include_stats?, include_suspend_reason?, include_card_image_badge?, etc.). ActiveModel::Serializer looks specifically for `include_<attr>?` to gate attribute serialization. As a result the predicate is never invoked and `website_name` is always included in the serialized JSON whenever the attribute is defined, regardless of the intended `website.present?` check. This also defeats any future attempt to gate website_name exposure (e.g. for TL0 users via untrusted_attributes, since the predicate won't fire).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the main issue in the golden comment: include_website_name is missing its '?' suffix, so conditional inclusion breaks. It does not mention the string concatenation point, but it matches the primary issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing test for the 'same suffix, equal part count > 2' branch

The new `website_name` implementation has three branches (exact match, `www.example.com == forum.example.com` style same-suffix with equal part count > 2, and parent-domain suffix). The spec only exercises the first and third (`Discourse.stubs(:current_hostname).returns('example.com')` and `...('forums.example.com')`); the elsif branch with two 3-part hosts sharing a suffix (e.g. `www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com`, both returning the full path) has no test, so a regression there would not be caught.

URI(website.to_s) parsed three times per call

`website_name` calls `URI(website.to_s)` three times to extract `.host` and `.path`. Since `website` is a method that reads `object.user_profile.website`, the value is stable across calls within one invocation, but parsing the URL three times is wasteful and makes the logic fragile: any future change that makes `website` non-deterministic (e.g., conditional computation) would cause `.host` and `.path` to be taken from different URLs. Hoisting `uri = URI(website.to_s)` (inside the existing `rescue`) into a local would fix both concerns.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses indexOf substring match

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` checks whether `e.origin` appears anywhere inside `discourseUrl` rather than comparing the origin exactly. Even though discourseUrl is configured by the embedding site, a confused deployer can be tricked into rejecting legitimate messages or accepting unexpected ones if the configured URL embeds other origins as substrings. Use `discourseUrl.startsWith(e.origin + '/')` or compare origins directly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the indexOf-based origin validation in the postMessage handler as insufficient and bypassable, and recommend exact origin comparison. The attack scenarios are described a little differently, but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer-based authorization is fragile and bypassable

`ensure_embeddable` only checks `URI(request.referer || '').host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The Referer header is freely spoofable in many environments (browsers with privacy extensions, server-side fetchers, embedded webviews, curl), it can be wholly absent (in which case the empty string still passes URI parsing and compares mismatched, denying the request), and the comparison is a plain string match that ignores ports/scheme. An attacker able to set Referer (or to load the embed URL from a non-browser context) can pretend to come from any host. Authorization must not rely on a header that the configured embeddable host cannot enforce, and should additionally match scheme/port (e.g. compare `host_with_port` and `scheme`). At minimum, the current check must be paired with a signed/shared-secret or signed embed_url before the controller will fetch arbitrary content from the Discourse server.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment has two parts: X-Frame-Options ALLOWALL disabling clickjacking protection, and the referer validation being bypassable, including the nil fallback. The candidate covers the second part: spoofable referer and the empty-string fallback. It does not mention X-Frame-Options. Since the referer bypass is a core part of the golden issue, this is a partial but substantive match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stored XSS via unescaped embed_url interpolated into raw_html post TopicEmbed#import builds a trailing reference by interpolating the caller-controlled url directly into an HTML attribute and text node: `contents << "
#{I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{url}")} "`. The url argument originates from arbitrary RSS items (PollFeed) or remote article fetches (import_remote), so an attacker controlling the feed/article can put characters like `'`, `>`, `"` into url to break out of the attribute or the link text. Because the contents are then stored as a post with `cook_method: raw_html` (which skips PrettyText/Markdown sanitization entirely, see app/models/post.rb#cook), the HTML is served verbatim to anyone rendering that post. Consequence: persistent XSS in Discourse via crafted RSS/ATOM items.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment names two problems: a NoMethodError when contents is nil, and XSS from the unescaped url interpolation. The candidate covers the XSS from the unescaped url in the generated HTML in detail. It does not mention the nil contents issue. Because it correctly identifies one of the two core issues in the same code line, it counts as a partial match on the same underlying problem.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError or encoding crash on RSS items missing content

`i.content.scrub` assumes `i.content` is a String that responds to scrub. SimpleRSS may leave `content` nil for entries without a `<content>` element, in which case the lookup raises NoMethodError on nil and aborts the entire poll (also no per-item rescue). On top of that, the surrounding code never validates the feed URL protocol, content type, or item count, and never catches network or parse errors, so a single malformed item or transient feed failure kills the whole job. Add nil guards (`i.content.to_s.scrub`) and per-item exception handling.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out that i.content.scrub raises NoMethodError when content is nil on RSS items that have no content element. The fixes differ (fallback to description vs a to_s guard), but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
XSS in embed layout: HTML-escaped referer inside a JS string literal

The postMessage call interpolates `request.referer` into a single-quoted JS string with `<%= request.referer %>`, which only HTML-escapes output. Inside `<script>`, HTML entities such as `'` are unescaped by the JS parser back to `'` before execution, so a parent page can supply a referer like `https://x'); alert(1); //` and execute attacker JS in the embed iframe. The whole script must be emitted with JS-string-escaping (CGI.escape / json_escape or equivalent) rather than the default HTML escape, e.g. by using `j` and a JSON-encoded value or by replacing `'` with `\'`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same issue: request.referer is interpolated into a JavaScript string without JS-appropriate escaping, which allows XSS. The candidate's claim that the JS parser decodes HTML entities inside a script tag is technically inaccurate, but it still identifies the same bug and location.

false_positives.candidate:
Migration backfills cook_method=1 (raw_html) for every post, breaking cooking pipeline

`add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false` sets the integer 1 as the default for all existing rows and for every future insert that omits cook_method. But `Post.cook_methods` is defined as `Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)` in app/models/post.rb, where the Enum assigns sequential indices starting at 0, so `:regular == 0` and `:raw_html == 1`. The migration therefore marks every existing post as raw_html. After deployment, `before_save` (`self.cooked = cook(raw, topic_id: topic_id) unless new_record?`) calls `Post#cook`, which now short-circuits to `return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, so the first edit on any previously-rendered post overwrites `cooked` with raw markdown and breaks rendering for that post and every post that quotes/redisplays it.

Post.cook short-circuits to raw_html because the migration default points at the raw_html enum value

`return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` is gated on the raw_html enum value, but the DB default set by the new migration (default: 1) and every PostCreator call that does not explicitly pass `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:regular]` will land on raw_html. Combined with the migration defaulting all rows to 1, every legacy post and every default-created post loses its cooked HTML. The intent appears to be that `raw_html` is opt-in (only the embed/RSS import path sets it), so the enum value used for the column default must be `:regular` (0) and any feed/import caller should pass the raw_html value explicitly. Right now, both kinds of writes converge on raw_html, corrupting posts.

TopicRetriever invokes scheduled feed poll synchronously inside an embed job

`Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` is called inline inside `perform_retrieve` whenever `SiteSetting.feed_polling_enabled?` is true. PollFeed is a recurring scheduled job that fetches the full configured RSS/ATOM feed and imports every item; running it synchronously inside an embed fetch blocks the worker for the full poll duration, doubles the load on the feed endpoint (once from the scheduled worker, once from each embed call), and re-imports items outside the dedup logic embedded in TopicEmbed.import. It should enqueue the scheduled job via Sidekiq or at minimum only check `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: ...)` without triggering a full re-poll.

NoMethodError when SiteSetting.embed_by_username is blank

`User.where(username_lower: SiteSetting.embed_by_username.downcase).first` calls `.downcase` on the setting value without first verifying it is non-nil. PollFeed guards against this with the `SiteSetting.embed_by_username.present?` check, but `TopicRetriever#fetch_http` does not, so a missing setting raises NoMethodError, which propagates out of the retrieve_topic job. Guard with `return if SiteSetting.embed_by_username.blank?` like PollFeed does.

force: true silently drops and recreates the top_topics table

Changing `create_table :top_topics` to `create_table :top_topics, force: true` makes the migration drop any pre-existing `top_topics` table before recreating it. The migration was previously already shipped to production; if any environment has a partially applied state, the next migration run will silently destroy data. Either drop the existing migration in favor of a new one that no-ops for upgrades, or document that this change must run on a clean DB only.

Unused require_dependency 'email/sender'

The job requires `email/sender` but never references it (and TopicRetriever does not either). Remove the unused dependency to avoid loading unnecessary code paths and to prevent surprising coupling when email/Sender changes.

Tests do not cover the perform_retrieve (SSRF and dedup) paths

The spec only exercises the gated path through `retrieve` and asserts that `perform_retrieve` is or isn't called. There is no coverage of `perform_retrieve`, `fetch_http`, the `Jobs::PollFeed` invocation, or the duplicate-embed short-circuit. SSRF (fetching arbitrary URLs via `import_remote`) and the dedup queries are security-/data-integrity-sensitive and should have explicit specs covering the host check inside perform_retrieve, the user lookup, and the `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url:).exists?` early-return.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedImage.downsize redefined from 4-arg to 3-arg form, silently breaking existing callers

The class method `OptimizedImage.downsize` is now defined twice in the same class. The second definition (`def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149) replaces the first one (`def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145), so the 4-argument form is gone. Any other caller in the codebase that still does `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, 800, 600)` (a 4-arg call with separate width/height integers) will now either raise ArgumentError or, worse, have its 4th argument silently bound to `opts` while `800` becomes the dimensions string, producing nonsensical ImageMagick commands like `-resize 800x`. This is a hidden API break in a helper that is used by thumbnail jobs and other places; the new signature should be a new method name (e.g. `downsize_to`) and the old 4-arg form should be preserved or deprecated explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem: downsize is defined twice, the second definition (a single dimensions parameter) overrides the first (separate max_width and max_height parameters), and existing callers that pass width and height separately break.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client upload size cap hardcoded to 10MB, bypassing the site setting

`validateUploadedFile` previously read the cap from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, supporting independent `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb`. It is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024` for every type. Consequences: (1) administrators lose the ability to tighten or loosen the client-side cap; (2) when an admin sets `max_image_size_kb` lower than 10MB the client still accepts up to 10MB and the user only finds out the upload is too large after the round trip; (3) the previous per-type distinction between images and attachments is lost. The site setting should still drive this value, or at minimum the hardcoded constant should be derived from the setting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the client-side size limit is hardcoded to 10MB and no longer reads the per-type site setting, so the client limit can diverge from the server. The candidate does not mention the 413 handler, but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
5 downsize iterations are mathematically insufficient for the feature to work

Each pass uses `"80%"` dimensions, which shrinks image area to 0.8² = 0.64 of the original, so the file size drops by roughly 36% per iteration. After 5 iterations the file is approximately 0.64⁵ ≈ 33% of the original. With the default `max_image_size_kb` of 10MB, any source image above ~30MB cannot be brought under the limit in 5 passes; for example a 50MB image ends up at ~16MB and a 100MB image at ~33MB. The `while` loop then exits and `Upload.create_for` is invoked with an oversized file, so the 'auto-downsize' feature silently fails for any but moderately large images. Either the iteration count must scale with the initial size, the reduction factor must be more aggressive, or the loop should compute the required scale per iteration and pass it to `OptimizedImage.downsize`.

413 error message shows hardcoded 10MB instead of configured limit

The 413 branch of `displayErrorForUpload` previously displayed `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` in the user-facing `file_too_large` error. It now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024`, so the size quoted in the error dialog no longer matches the actual configured `max_image_size_kb`. Users will see '10MB' even when the real limit is 2MB or 50MB, leading to confusing UX after any admin change to the site setting.

In-place downsize overwrites source file and ignores failure

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` reads from and writes to the same path. If the convert/gifsicle invocation fails (corrupt input, OOM, signal, bad permissions), ImageMagick may truncate or zero out the file before erroring, and the loop never checks the return value (`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns true/false), so the next iteration or the subsequent `Upload.create_for` will run on a corrupted/empty file. The fix is to write to a separate temp path, verify the result, then atomically rename, and to break out of the loop when downsize reports failure rather than blindly iterating again.

URL download cap is a hardcoded 10MB, no longer tied to max_image_size_kb

`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces the previous cap of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. With a 60-minute event this can return bookable slots that extend past the organizer's day.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

Dayjs objects compared with === instead of isSame

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly-constructed Dayjs objects with strict equality. Dayjs objects are compared by reference, so this branch is unreachable. The intent appears to be "override has zero duration / is empty", which should be `…isSame(…)`. Consequence: an empty/zero-length date override is never short-circuited and the surrounding code falls through to the other boundary checks, which can produce wrong availability when start and end coincide.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug: dayjs objects are compared with ===, which checks references and so is always false. Both recommend using isSame instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours day/hour/minute read from UTC, not organizer tz

`slotStartTime` is `time.utc()`, so `slotStartTime.day()`, `.hour()` and `.minute()` return UTC values, while `workingHours` are stored in the organizer's timezone. The membership check `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` and the minute comparison will be wrong near day boundaries or for organizers not in UTC (e.g. a slot at 23:30 IST = 18:00 UTC will be checked against the UTC day/hour instead of the IST day/hour). This can return slots outside the organizer's working day or filter out slots that should be available.

Date-override day match is compared in UTC, not organizer tz

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` compares two UTC-formatted dates. The date override is a calendar day in the organizer's timezone, and `slotStartTime` is in UTC. Around the day boundary (e.g. override on 2024-01-01 IST = 2023-12-31 18:30 UTC …) a slot on the correct local day can be compared against the wrong UTC date and the override will be silently ignored. Use the organizer's timezone for both sides of the comparison (e.g. `dayjs.tz(slotStartTime, organizerTimeZone).format(...)`).

Override boundary check is strict, missing same-instant starts

`slotStartTime.isAfter(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` is strict: a slot whose start equals the override end is not filtered, and slots that straddle the override end (e.g. override 14:00–18:00, slot 17:30–18:30) are also not filtered because there is no check that the slot end is within the override. The check should also require `slotStartTime` not to be after `date.end` (use `isSameOrAfter` or also verify the slot end) and the same boundary issue applies to `date.start` (a slot that begins before the override starts but ends inside it slips through).

checkIfIsAvailable ignores override.timeZone, uses caller-supplied organizerTimeZone

`dateOverrides` are flattened with `timeZone: availability.timeZone` attached, but `checkIfIsAvailable`'s signature drops that field (type is `{ start: Date; end: Date }[]`) and instead uses the caller-supplied `organizerTimeZone` to compute the UTC offset for `date.start`. If a date override was created in a timezone different from the one currently passed as `organizerTimeZone` (e.g. round-robin where a fixed host's override was stored with one tz and `schedule.timeZone` resolves to another, or DST boundary), the override's intended local time will be misinterpreted, returning the wrong availability.

override.start.toString() parsed in server local tz, then re-zoned

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` first stringifies a Date (which embeds the server's local timezone offset) and parses it back, then re-zones. The resulting `utcOffset` depends on the server's TZ rather than being a pure UTC interpretation. On any server not running in UTC the organizer/invitee offset values (and therefore the computed `offset` and the resulting `startTime`/`endTime`) will be wrong. Use `dayjs.utc(override.start)` (or pass the Date directly) before `.tz(...)`.

override startTime/endTime computed in UTC, not invitee local time

`dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + …` produces the hour/minute of the shifted UTC instant, but the surrounding `buildSlots` compares these values to `dayStart` which is in the invitee's local timezone. The result is that for two invitees in different timezones the same `startTime` value yields the same UTC slot, regardless of invitee tz. This is exactly the behavior the PR description claims to fix ("date overrides didn't adjust to different timezones"). The correct computation is the override's start in the invitee's local tz, e.g. `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).hour() * 60 + dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).minute()`.

The new `scheduleForEventOnADayWithDateOverrideDifferentTimezone` case calls `getSchedule` with `timeZone: "Asia/Dhaka"` and expects the identical UTC slots `[08:30, 09:30, 10:30, 11:30]` as the IST case, with the comment "it should return the same as this is the utc time". The PR description says the fix makes date overrides adjust to the attendee's timezone, so two invitees in materially different timezones (e.g. IST vs America/Los_Angeles) should see different UTC slots. The test as written locks in the pre-fix behavior and will not catch a regression of the stated bug; it also only spans a 30-minute tz difference which doesn't expose the problem at all.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No guard against concurrent cron execution; duplicate SMS and lost retryCount increments possible

The handler reads `unscheduledReminders`, calls the external `twilio.scheduleSMS`, and then updates `workflowReminder` in separate non-transactional steps. There is no lock, advisory mutex, or single-runner coordination. If two cron instances overlap (e.g., the previous run is still in flight when a new one starts, or this cron is invoked manually while a scheduled run is active), both will fetch the same unscheduled rows, both will call `twilio.scheduleSMS` (producing duplicate SMS messages for end users), and both will perform `update` based on the same `retryCount` snapshot so one increment is effectively a no-op. The newly added retry logic amplifies this: if retryCount increments are lost due to the race, a reminder may need more than 2 actual failures before being cleaned up, or conversely may be deleted after only one observed failure. At minimum, the handler should use an advisory lock keyed on the workflow step or use an idempotent update (`update where retryCount = <stale value>`) to make the increment safe.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies lost retryCount increments caused by concurrent updates that use a stale snapshot, and it suggests a safe increment. This is the same race condition the golden comment describes, though the candidate frames it more broadly.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

deleteMany retryCount branch lacks method filter, can delete non-SMS reminders

The new OR clause in the cleanup deleteMany only filters by `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` on the second branch, with no `method` constraint. The first branch correctly restricts to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`, but the retryCount branch will match WorkflowReminder rows of any method (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) if their retryCount ever exceeds 1. While this PR only increments retryCount for SMS, this is a latent bug: any future code path (or out-of-band DB change) that pushes an EMAIL/WHATSAPP reminder's retryCount above 1 will cause it to be silently deleted by this SMS handler. The retry branch should be `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` to keep the cleanup semantically consistent with the rest of the handler, which only processes SMS.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. The retryCount branch of the OR clause in the deleteMany has no method: SMS filter, so non-SMS reminders (Email, WhatsApp) with retryCount > 1 can be deleted. Both propose the same fix of adding the SMS method filter to that branch.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests cover the new retry-count / cleanup behavior

The change introduces new persistence logic (a new column, conditional increment in two branches, and a new cleanup predicate) but no test files were added or updated. There is no coverage verifying: (a) `retryCount` is incremented when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy, (b) `retryCount` is incremented in the catch branch, (c) reminders with `retryCount > 1` are deleted regardless of scheduledDate, (d) past-dated SMS reminders without retries are still deleted, or (e) the off-by-one threshold (2 failures -> delete) matches the PR description. Without tests, regressions in the retry threshold or in the OR-clause semantics (e.g., the missing method filter noted above) can ship undetected.

The catch block logs only `Error scheduling SMS with error ${error}`. It does not include the reminder id, booking uid, workflowStepId, scheduledDate, sendTo, or the prior retryCount value. When the new retry-and-delete flow drops a reminder (after retryCount > 1) there is no operator-visible trail of which reminder was deleted or why it was abandoned, which makes production debugging and audit of dropped SMS reminders very difficult. The new OR clause causes any WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 to be deleted regardless of its scheduledDate. This matches the PR description but is worth flagging: there is no alerting or metric when a future reminder is given up on, and no way to distinguish "transient Twilio failure" from "permanent bad phone number". Minimum token schema is malformed and does not validate anything

The schema is declared as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. `z.string().toString()` evaluates to the literal string `"z.string()"` and Zod's `z.object` does not support arbitrary computed keys this way — it emits a warning at schema construction and the dynamic entries do not actually constrain any property. The resulting schema is effectively `{ access_token: string }` with an additional unknown catch-all, so `refresh_token`, `expiry_date`, `expires_in`, scopes, etc. are not enforced. The function should instead take the provider-specific `schema` argument when credential sharing is enabled (since the shared endpoint returns whatever format the host chose) or declare the real required fields.

The next time `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` runs it will throw and the credential will be unusable. Other integrations (`office365calendar`, `salesforce`, `zoomvideo`, `webex`) correctly do `...tokenResponse.data` or `...parsedToken.data` — only googlecalendar was updated incorrectly.

false_positives.candidate:
Webhook handler accepts any HTTP method

The handler does not check `req.method` before processing. Combined with no CSRF protection and a single shared secret, this lets an attacker who learns the secret invoke the endpoint via GET (which Next.js does not JSON-parse by default, so `reqBody = z.parse(undefined)` will throw a 500), or submit via PUT/DELETE which could also expose side effects. The endpoint should explicitly require POST and reject other methods with 405.

Unprotected JSON.parse after decrypt can crash the request

`symmetricDecrypt` returns the raw decrypted bytes and the result is fed directly into `JSON.parse` with no try/catch. If the symmetric decrypt throws (bad key, tampered ciphertext, wrong padding) or the plaintext is not valid JSON, the handler crashes with an uncaught exception and returns a generic 500 instead of a 4xx. This also means the webhook secret check, user existence check, etc. cannot return a proper error. The decrypt and parse should be wrapped, and the result should be validated as an object before being assigned to `key`.

findFirst-then-create is racy and can duplicate credentials

The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ userId, appId })` followed by `update` or `create` with no transaction. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same (userId, appId) can both observe no existing credential and both insert, leaving two `Credential` rows that downstream code (which does `findFirst` in e.g. office365video callback) cannot reliably deduplicate. Use `prisma.credential.upsert` with a unique compound key, or wrap the read/write in a transaction with appropriate isolation.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality

The webhook secret is compared with `!==`. Although the secret is shared and not user-derived, attackers can in principle exploit timing differences to recover the secret byte by byte. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` against buffers of equal length (after a length check) to close this side channel.

Credential type sourced from app metadata, not the request

When creating a credential, the code uses `appMetadata.type` for `type` while the existing callbacks elsewhere in the codebase store values like `"google_calendar"`, `"hubspot_other_calendar"`, `"office365_video"`, etc. If `appStoreMetadata`'s `type` differs from the conventional string used elsewhere for the same app (or if the DB `app` row's slug does not match the metadata entry's slug), the new credential's `type` column will not match what CalendarService implementations later filter on, causing the freshly synced credential to be ignored.

Outgoing credential-sync POST has no authentication

When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, this function POSTs `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` to the configured endpoint with no auth header. The receiving endpoint cannot verify the request came from this Cal.com instance, and a network attacker (or anyone who knows the endpoint URL) can impersonate arbitrary Cal.com users to obtain refreshed tokens. The same `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (and matching header name) that the incoming webhook requires should be sent on this outgoing request.

Salesforce getClient refreshes the OAuth token on every instantiation

`getClient` now unconditionally POSTs to the Salesforce token endpoint on every call, then writes the response to the DB. Previously Salesforce never did a refresh in this code path; every connection was constructed from the stored `credentialKey`. With the new code each `CalendarService` construction (and therefore each event create/update/getAvailability cycle that goes through the manager) makes an extra network round trip and a DB write. Add an expiry check before refreshing, matching the patterns used by googlecalendar / hubspot / webex.

APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean

`export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` evaluates to the encryption-key string when both env vars are set, or to `undefined`/`""` otherwise. Call sites use it in `if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)` (truthy check), which works in practice, but it is documented/used as a boolean flag. Coerce explicitly: `Boolean(process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY)` so the type matches usage and an empty-string secret cannot accidentally enable sharing.

JSON.parse on req.query.state has no error handling

`JSON.parse(req.query.state)` will throw a SyntaxError if the state parameter is not valid JSON, turning the OAuth `add` endpoint into a 500. This code path is exercised only on path renames in this PR, but the file was moved and is part of the changed set; a `try`/`catch` returning `undefined` (matching the early-return for non-string state) would be safer. Same issue in `decodeOAuthState.ts`.

New webhook has no tests despite being the trust boundary for cross-instance credentials

The endpoint accepts encrypted credentials that fully overwrite a user's third-party OAuth tokens (potentially including refresh tokens) for any app, gated only by a single shared secret. The PR description acknowledges no tests were added. At minimum: tests for wrong/missing secret (403), unknown user (404), unknown app (404), invalid encrypted payload (4xx, not 500), missing/short encryption key, and concurrent writes for the same (userId, appId) should exist before merge.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
try/catch around forEach with awaited async work is dead code

`originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach(...)` calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...)` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` without `await`, and both helpers internally wrap their work in try/catch and only log errors. No error from those calls can ever propagate into the surrounding `catch (error)` block at line 970, so the `log.error(...)` is unreachable for any real failure. This is misleading and hides the fact that the caller has no way to know whether a reminder was successfully cancelled. Either `await` each call inside a per-iteration try/catch, or have the helpers rethrow and the caller await them.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate points out that deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach during rescheduling. It also says the caller cannot know whether a reminder was actually cancelled, and it recommends awaiting the calls. This is the same underlying issue as the golden comment, even though the candidate frames it around the dead try/catch.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteScheduledEmailReminder immediateDelete path leaves DB unupdated

When `immediateDelete` is true, the function calls the SendGrid cancel API and then returns without updating or deleting the WorkflowReminder row in the database. The two other code paths (`!referenceId` and `immediateDelete === false`) both clean up the DB row, so this branch is inconsistent. As a result, callers using `immediateDelete=true` (e.g. reschedules in `handleNewBooking.ts`) leave orphan rows in `WorkflowReminder` that will only be cleaned up once `scheduledDate` is in the past. More importantly, because the row is never marked `cancelled=true`, the CRON in `scheduleEmailReminders.ts` (which only selects `where: { cancelled: true }`) cannot retry the SendGrid cancellation if the initial API call fails, so the original SendGrid problem (failed cancellations → emails still being sent) is only partially fixed. The fix is either to also set `cancelled: true` (or delete the row) in this branch, or to stop passing `immediateDelete=true` from callers where this matters (such as the reschedule path, which unlike the workflow delete path does not rely on a cascade to remove the row).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the same thing: when immediateDelete is true, the SendGrid email is cancelled but the WorkflowReminder DB record is never deleted or updated. Both note this leaves orphaned rows and is inconsistent with the other code paths. The golden comment's extra point about the omitted SendGrid DELETE call is minor, and the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Reschedule uses immediateDelete=true, bypassing the new deferred-cancel mechanism

When a booking is rescheduled, the workflow reminders of the original booking are cancelled by calling `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)`. This is inconsistent with the new design (which only marks `cancelled=true` and lets the CRON actually cancel in SendGrid) and with the cancellation flow in `handleCancelBooking.ts`, which calls the same function without `immediateDelete`. Because `immediateDelete=true` does not mark the row `cancelled=true`, the CRON never picks it up and there is no retry if SendGrid's `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` fails — exactly the failure mode this PR is trying to fix. Reschedules will therefore continue to send the original reminder whenever SendGrid has any transient issue. The call should drop the third argument and rely on the same deferred approach as `handleCancelBooking.ts`.

Catch block aborts all SendGrid cancellations on a single failure

The try/catch wraps the entire `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop. A single SendGrid API failure (4xx/5xx, network error, rate limit, etc.) aborts the loop and skips every subsequent cancellation in this CRON run, even though the per-iteration `await client.request(...)` and `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` are independent. There is also no partial cleanup: if the throw happens after some `workflowReminder.delete` calls have been pushed but before `await Promise.all(...)`, those prisma operations are left as fire-and-forget unhandled promises. The catch should be moved inside the loop so one failed reminder doesn't stop the rest, and the deletes should be awaited per iteration (or collected only after a successful cancel).

Cancellation query does not filter by method

`prisma.workflowReminder.findMany` selects reminders where `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate <= now + 1h` but does not restrict to `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. Today only EMAIL reminders are marked `cancelled=true` (SMS reminders are deleted immediately via `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`), so this is latent, but the cron then unconditionally calls SendGrid's `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `batch_id: reminder.referenceId` on whatever it finds. If a future change ever marks an SMS reminder as cancelled, this code will try to cancel it via the email provider and may also `delete` it, losing the row. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` to the where clause for safety.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

This means the user must be BOTH admin AND owner to be granted permission. A team admin (who is not an owner) is incorrectly denied. The variable name and intent clearly indicate either role should be sufficient. Compare with the rest of the codebase where similar checks use `||`. As written, almost no legitimate user passes this branch unless they happen to be both.

Client-side uniqueness/email validation is misleading and not exhaustive

The schema is `z.array(z.string().email()).refine(... unique ...)`, and a failed parse just sets `isInvalidEmail` and shows the generic 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' message. Initial state is `[""]`, so the dialog is invalid out of the box; the message does not indicate which entry is bad, nor does it surface the empty-string case specifically. That is the same underlying issue as the golden comment: an empty-string initial value causing validation problems. The candidate also raises other concerns, but this point is covered.

false_positives.candidate:
Any existing attendee can add arbitrary third parties to a booking

Authorization allows the request if the user is the organizer OR an attendee:

```ts
const isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find((attendee) => attendee.email === user.email);
if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) { ... }
```

Combined with the dialog's unrestricted email entry, any original invitee can inject any third-party email into the booking, getting them full calendar details, organizer info, other attendees, and a meeting invitation without the organizer's consent. The organizer should normally be the only one (plus team admins/owners) permitted to add guests. This is a serious privacy/access-control issue.

Guests persisted to DB before calendar/email side-effects, with no rollback

The flow is: `prisma.booking.update` (commits new attendees) -> `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` -> `sendAddGuestsEmails` (wrapped only in a `console.log` on error). There is no transaction and no compensation. If `updateCalendarAttendees` throws (e.g., bad credentials, video provider error), the guests remain in the database but never receive an invite; the caller sees a TRPC error and may retry, creating duplicates. If email sending fails it is silently swallowed, so the UI reports success while the new guest never receives notification. Either wrap everything in a transaction with rollback, or reverse the order (validate-then-side-effect-then-persist) and surface failures properly.

Allows adding guests to cancelled or already-completed bookings

After loading the booking there is no check on `booking.status`. A user can add guests to a `CANCELLED`, `REJECTED`, or past `ACCEPTED` booking. `sendAddGuestsEmails` will still send a 'guests added' notification and `updateCalendarAttendees` will still push an updated invite for an event that is no longer happening. Guard against `booking.status === BookingStatus.CANCELLED` (and arguably against bookings in the past).

New guests are inserted with empty name and the organizer's timezone/locale

Each new guest row is created with:

```ts
{ name: "", email: guest, timeZone: organizer.timeZone, locale: organizer.locale }
```

An empty `name` will render as a blank attendee in the UI (booking list, emails, calendar) and confuses no-show/dropdown flows. Also forcing the organizer's timezone/locale means the new guest's localized email content and meeting-time display are wrong. Either ask for a name in the dialog (it currently does not), or at minimum leave name nullable/derive a placeholder, and use a sensible default locale (e.g., `en`).

`booking?.userPrimaryEmail` is not a known Booking field

The calendar event uses `email: booking?.userPrimaryEmail ?? organizer.email`. The Prisma `Booking` model exposes `user` (relation) and `userId`, but I cannot find a `userPrimaryEmail` column on the Booking model in this diff's context. If it doesn't exist on `booking`, this will be `undefined` and the fallback `organizer.email` is used; otherwise the column may silently return `null` and bypass the intended primary-email selection. Verify the field exists; if not, drop the `??` or fetch from the user relation explicitly.

addGuests uses authedProcedure instead of bookingsProcedure

All sibling booking mutations in this router (`editLocation`) are wrapped with `bookingsProcedure` which presumably enforces booking-level authorization. `addGuests` uses the bare `authedProcedure`, leaving all access control to the handler. The handler has the permission bugs described above, so any logged-in user who can hit this endpoint relies entirely on a handler bug-free. Switch to `bookingsProcedure` for consistency and defense-in-depth.

Uses array index as React key for email fields

`value.map((field, index) => <li key={index}>...)`. When a user removes an item in the middle of the list, every input after it is re-bound to the wrong value (because React reuses the DOM and state by index). Use a stable key (e.g., the email value itself or a generated id) so removing index N doesn't corrupt the remaining inputs.

No automated tests for a new permission-sensitive mutation with email and calendar side-effects

The PR adds a new tRPC mutation `viewer.bookings.addGuests` that mutates the DB, calls calendar/video integrations, and dispatches emails. There are no unit tests, integration tests, or e2e tests included. Given the multiple authorization bugs (admin+owner check, attendee-as-actor, case-sensitive dedupe, wrong credentials) and side-effect ordering issues already found in this review, at minimum a test suite covering: (1) team admin can add, team member cannot; (2) attendee cannot add; (3) case-insensitive duplicate is rejected; (4) cancelled booking is rejected; (5) calendar/email failures are surfaced, must be added before merge.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Race condition lets backup codes be reused / resurrected

The backup-code branch decrypts user.backupCodes, finds the matching index, sets the slot to null, and then writes the array back (lines 139-156). The read-decrypt-mutate-write cycle is non-atomic. If two concurrent authorize() calls hit it with the same backup code, both will decrypt the original array, both will find the match, and both will mark the slot null — so the same one-time code authenticates twice. With two different backup codes, each call mutates its own copy and the later write overwrites the earlier one, resurrecting the code that the first request already consumed. Because authorize() runs on every NextAuth credentials sign-in, a user with stolen credentials (or a session race) could keep re-using the same backup code. Replace the in-memory mutation with a single conditional Prisma update (e.g. a JSONB / array-element update that removes only the matched code) so the consumption is atomic at the database level.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same issue. The non-atomic decrypt-mutate-write of backupCodes lets two concurrent requests both accept the same backup code, which breaks one-time use.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blob URL leaks until next setup round-trip

`setBackupCodesUrl(URL.createObjectURL(textBlob))` is called on every setup response but the URL is only revoked when a *subsequent* setup response arrives. If the user reaches the backup codes screen and then closes the dialog (Cancel / Close) or the parent component unmounts without re-running setup, the latest object URL is never revoked. Combined with `resetState()` not clearing `backupCodesUrl`, opening the modal again can also bind to a stale URL. Revoke the previous URL inside `resetState` and on a `useEffect` cleanup that fires when the modal closes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: the backup codes object URL is never revoked when the component unmounts or the dialog closes, so it leaks memory. The candidate explicitly covers the unmount case and suggests revoking it in a useEffect cleanup.

false_positives.candidate:
Disable endpoint has no rate limiting on backup-code guesses

The disable endpoint verifies password (bcrypt-bounded) and then accepts a backup code by `backupCodes.indexOf(req.body.backupCode.replaceAll('-', ''))`. Unlike the NextAuth credentials authorize flow, this endpoint does NOT call `checkRateLimitAndThrowError`. An attacker who already has the user's password can therefore brute-force the ten 10-hex-char backup codes at full speed (only bcrypt on the password limits them, and that throttling is per user, not per attempt). The endpoint also never marks the consumed code, so even a correct guess leaves the rest usable. Add a rate limit per (userId, IP) and reuse the atomic consumption pattern from the credentials authorize flow.

All-codes-exhausted state is indistinguishable from a typo

When a user has consumed every backup code, `backupCodes` is `[null, null, ..., null]`. `user.backupCodes` is still a non-empty encrypted string, so the `if (!user.backupCodes) throw MissingBackupCodes` guard never fires. The user instead gets `IncorrectBackupCode` on every attempt, with no way to tell that they've actually run out of codes. After decrypt+parse, detect the case where every element is null/missing and throw `MissingBackupCodes` (or a new dedicated error) so the UI can surface a clear message and the user knows to re-enable 2FA and regenerate codes.

Backup-code login and disable paths are not end-to-end tested

The new e2e additions only exercise the backup-codes dialog (download/copy/close) after enabling 2FA. The two security-critical paths this PR introduces — logging in via backup code from `apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx` (`twoFactorLostAccess` flow) and disabling 2FA via the 'Lost access' path in `DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx` — have no test at all. The PR description itself acknowledges 'I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective'. For an authentication feature, both the happy path and the wrong-code / exhausted-code negative paths must be covered, and the consumed-once invariant should be asserted (e.g. login with the same code twice, second attempt must fail).

resetState leaves isSubmitting, backupCodes, secret and dataUri in place

`resetState()` only clears `password`, `errorMessage`, and `step`. It does not reset `isSubmitting`, `backupCodes`, `backupCodesUrl` (blob URL — see separate finding), `dataUri`, or `secret`. If the modal is closed and reopened, the next 'Continue' button can stay disabled (because `isSubmitting` may still be true from a previous round), and the stale `secret` / `dataUri` could be displayed against a brand-new secret if the user races the step transitions. Reset all transient state and revoke any pending blob URL inside `resetState`.

body.backupCodes assumed to be present and a string array

Right after `await response.json()`, the code does `body.backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode)` with no guard. If the server ever returns an error body that lacks `backupCodes`, or returns it under a different key, or with non-string elements, the page crashes mid-setup and `setIsSubmitting(false)` runs but the user is left on a broken step. Validate the shape (Array.isArray and every element is a string) before using it, and fall back to the existing `something_went_wrong` error if it isn't.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateEvent fallback always returns undefined

The new fallback `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` is reached only when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so the predicate searches for `cal.externalId === undefined`, which never matches. The previous behavior was `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` (a valid fallback). Now `selectedCalendar` is undefined when externalCalendarId is omitted, and there is no `'primary'` fallback like `createEvent` has — the update is sent to `calendarId: undefined`, which Google rejects. This breaks updates for any booking whose stored `externalCalendarId` is null (notably pre-refactor bookings created before references existed).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same buggy line: the destinationCalendar find predicate compares cal.externalId to externalCalendarId, a self-referential lookup that fails. The golden describes it as matching a calendar against itself. The candidate says the fallback runs when externalCalendarId is falsy, so it searches for undefined and never matches. The framing differs slightly, but the underlying logic error and location are the same.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteEvent fallback always returns undefined

Same bug as in updateEvent: the find-against-undefined pattern guarantees no match, so `calendarId` falls back to 'primary' regardless of where the event actually lives. Result: deleteEvent targets a calendar that doesn't contain the event, returning 404, and the `if (err.code === 404) return resolve();` handler silently swallows the failure. Real deletion therefore never occurs for legacy bookings where `externalCalendarId` is null.

TypeError when MeetLocationType has no destination calendar

`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` produces `undefined` when the array is empty/absent. The very next line reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration`, which throws on `undefined`. Previously this was guarded by `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`, so picking 'Google Meet' for any user without a destination calendar (a routine configuration) now 500s the booking instead of falling back to Cal Video.

Recurring cancellation uses booking owner's credentials only

Inside the recurring-event branch the code re-iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(c => c.type.endsWith('_calendar'))` rather than the credential already resolved for the current reference. For collective bookings the booking owner is only one of several hosts; the other hosts' calendar credentials live elsewhere in the database (the if-branch already handles this by falling back to `prisma.credential.findUnique`). Only using the owner's calendars means other hosts' recurring instances never get deleted. The inner loop should be driven by `updBooking.references`/`reference.credentialId`, not by the owner's credentials.

Falls back to empty instead of user's destination calendar

`destinationCalendar: bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar ? [...] : []` lost the user-level fallback present everywhere else. Every other handler in this PR (confirm, editLocation, handleCancelBooking, deleteCredential, paypal-webhook, stripe webhook) falls back to `user.destinationCalendar` when the booking has none. Pre-reschedule bookings with no destination calendar will now be sent through reschedule emails and reschedule webhooks with `destinationCalendar: []`, and EventManager then has no host calendar to invite, which can produce no calendar events for the requester.

loadUsers refactor drops organization select

The new `loadUsers` removed `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the dynamic-user branch. Any downstream code that reads the user's organization slug from the loaded user (including the post-load flow that may construct event URLs / emails / org-aware flows) will receive `undefined`. The original select surfaced organization data so removing it is a silent regression, not a cleanup.

loadUsers error wrapping loses original status/context

Any error (including the new dynamicUserList-empty check) is rethrown as HttpError 500 'Unable to load users' unless it is already a Prisma error. This both changes observable behavior (a previously-silent empty dynamicUserList now turns into a 500 booking failure) and hides the real cause in logs. The empty-dynamicUserList guard should not be treated like a server failure.

Inconsistent empty destinationCalendar value across handlers

handleNewBooking emits `destinationCalendar: null` when both eventType and organizer have no destination calendar, while every other handler updated in this PR (confirm, editLocation, cancel, payment webhooks, deleteCredential, bookingReminder) emits `destinationCalendar: []` in the same case. Consumers (webhooks, emails, calendar services that do `[mainHost] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []`) now have to handle both shapes for the same 'no calendar' semantic. Pick one (preferably `[]`) and apply it everywhere.

Booking create no longer persists per-host references when result.externalId is missing

In `create()` the new code sets `externalCalendarId: result.externalId` and `credentialId: result.credentialId` for calendar references. The `else` branch in `createAllCalendarEvents` (when `destination.credentialId` is undefined) calls `createEvent(c, event)` without the third `externalId` argument, so `result.externalId` is undefined, and the new reference is created with an undefined `externalCalendarId`. Later updates/deletes on those references will not target any specific calendar and will fall back to 'primary' / fail. With the new multi-host flow this branch is also reachable for brand-new collective bookings if any destination entry lacks a credentialId.

Unrelated logic change mixed into destinationCalendar PR

The diff inverts the original `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug }` / `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { requestedSlug: slug }` into ternaries. This is a real bug fix (the original logic put `slug` on the org when billing was disabled, which is almost certainly wrong) but it is completely unrelated to the destinationCalendar array migration. It is a maintainability concern: bundling behavioral fixes in unrelated PRs makes bisecting and reverting harder, and this PR does not document or test the new behavior.

Booking-references loop runs delete logic serially before any awaits

The outer `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` does multiple sequential awaits per iteration: a Prisma `findUnique` for the credential, then possibly another to get a calendar, then `deleteEvent`. With multiple calendar references (collective bookings), this serializes N round-trips before any deletes actually fire. The deleteEvent calls themselves are collected as promises and awaited together later (`Promise.allSettled(...apiDeletes)`), so they are parallel, but the credential/calendar lookups preceding them are not. For a 5-host collective this turns into 5 sequential DB reads per cancellation. Hoist `prisma.credential.findUnique` lookups into a `Promise.all` and only await `getCalendar` after, or cache by id.

schedulingType added to CalendarEvent but unused

A new `schedulingType?: SchedulingType | null` field is added to `CalendarEvent`, and `handleNewBooking.ts` writes it onto `evt`. No consumer in this diff (or elsewhere in the codebase per the changes shown) reads it, and there is no documentation explaining which calendar integrations are expected to key off it. It is purely dead surface area — either remove it until a consumer exists or commit the consumer together with this PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach(async ...) does not await calendar/video deletions

The code wraps the bookingRef iteration in `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })`. `Array.prototype.forEach` ignores the return value of its callback and does not await Promises, so the async callbacks (which now `await getCalendar(...)` and invoke `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` / `deleteMeeting(...)`) are fire-and-forget. The outer `Reschedule` function returns as soon as the synchronous work completes, before the calendar/video integrations have been cancelled. Previously these were synchronous calls; the async refactor turned them into background tasks. The booking row is updated to CANCELLED and `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` is awaited before these deletions actually run, which is a data-integrity regression (integrations can stay in sync with the old time slot after the DB has already been flipped). Replace the `forEach` with a sequential `for...of` (or `Promise.all(refs.map(...))`) so the deletions are awaited.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug: forEach with async callbacks makes the calendar/video deletions fire-and-forget because they are never awaited. Both also recommend the same fix, using for...of or Promise.all with map.

false_positives.candidate:
forEach(async ...) does not await calendar/video deletions

Identical antipattern to vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })`. After making the inner callback async, forEach no longer awaits any of the calendar `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting` Promises. The `Reschedule` function continues running and the `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` is awaited before the integration deletions actually execute. Result: the booking is updated, the reschedule email goes out, and the function returns before the previous Google/Outlook/Zoom events are cancelled. Convert to a real awaited loop.

forEach(async ...) skips calendar/video cancellations on reschedule

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` does not await the async callback. Inside, the code `await`s `getCalendar(...)` and calls `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` and `deleteMeeting(...)`, but because forEach discards the returned Promise and does not block, the `requestReschedule` mutation can finish — sending `sendRequestRescheduleEmail`, webhooks, and returning to the caller — before any of the previous calendar/video entries are cancelled. Previously these calls were synchronous; the async conversion silently turned them into best-effort background work. Replace with `for (const bookingRef of bookingRefsFiltered) { ... }` or `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.
